<snippet id="39594183">Title: Sequential Diagnostic Approach Using FIB-4 and ELF for Predicting Advanced Fibrosis in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease.
Authors: Kang, Yeo-Wool, Baek, Yang-Hyun, Moon, Sang-Yi | Year: 2024 | Journal: Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)
Abstract: Background and Aims : Multiple non-invasive tests (NITs) for identifying advanced fibrosis in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) are available, but, due to the limitations of single NITs, the American Association for the Study of Liver Disease (AASLD) guidelines suggest a two-step strategy, combining the Fibrosis-4 Index (FIB-4) score with the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) test to improve diagnostic accuracy and minimize unnecessary liver biopsies. However, few real-world studies have used such a sequential approach. We here evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of the ELF test in patients with recently established metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and assessed the clinical utility of applying a two-step strategy, including the ELF test following the FIB-4 score assessment, in patients with MASLD. Methods : We enrolled 153 patients diagnosed with MASLD who underwent liver biopsy at the Dong-A University Hospital between June 2018 and August 2023. The degree of fibrosis was determined based on liver biopsy results. Various NITs were used, including the Aminotransferase-to-Platelet Ratio Index (APRI), FIB-4 score, NAFLD Fibrosis score (NFS) and ELF test. The diagnostic efficacy of these NITs was evaluated based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Additionally, the performance of each test was further examined both when applied individually and in a two-step approach, where FIB-4 was used followed by ELF testing. Key metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and accuracy were used for this analysis. Results : Overall, 153 patients with MASLD (mean age: 46.62 years; 52.3% men; 28.1% with type 2 diabetes) were included. The performance of the NITs in identifying advanced fibrosis was as follows: the AUROC of the APRI, FIB-4, NFS, and ELF tests were 0.803 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.713-0.863), 0.769 (95% CI, 0.694-0.833), 0.699 (95% CI, 0.528-0.796), and 0.829 (95% CI, 0.760-0.885), respectively. The combination of the FIB-4 score ≥ 1.30 and the ELF score ≥ 9.8 showed 67.86% sensitivity, 90.40% specificity, a PPV of 75.18%, an NPV of 86.78%, an accuracy of 83.64%, and an AUROC of 0.791 for predicting the diagnosis of advanced fibrosis. This approach excluded 28 patients (71.8%) from unnecessary liver biopsies. Conclusions : Our study demonstrated that ELF testing maintained diagnostic accuracy in assessing liver fibrosis in patients with MASLD in real-world practice. This test was used as a second step in the evaluation, reducing clinically unnecessary invasive liver biopsies and referrals to tertiary institutions. This approach allows assessment of MASLD severity in primary care settings without requiring additional equipment.</snippet>
<snippet id="35558366">Title: Non-Invasive Diagnostic Test for Advanced Fibrosis in Adolescents With Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease.
Authors: Mosca, Antonella, Della Volpe, Luca, Alisi, Anna et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Frontiers in pediatrics
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a multifaceted disease that includes a wide spectrum of liver damage. The presence and the degree of fibrosis are considered important factors for the prognosis of NAFLD and in predicting the risk of developing cirrhosis. Our aim was to evaluate the usefulness of four fibrosis scores (aspartate aminotransferase/Platelet Index [APRI], FIB-4, NAFLD Fibrosis Score [NFS], and Hepamet) in predicting different degrees of fibrosis among children with biopsy-proven NAFLD.
METHODS
About 286 adolescents [mean age 14.3 years ± 2.5; 154 (53.6%) males], referred between January 2014 and December 2019, with biopsy-proven NAFLD were enrolled.
RESULTS
About 173 (60.4%) patients presented fibrosis at histological analysis. In particular: 140 (49.3%) patients had F = 1, 31 (10.8%), had F = 2 and 2 (0.66%) had F = 3. APRI (AUROC 0.619, 95% CI 0.556-0.679) and Hepamet (AUROC 0.778, 95% CI 0.722-0.828) scores had significant ( p < 0.001) accuracy to distinguish subjects with fibrosis; while NFS and FIB-4 had not. APRI had a positive predictive value (PPV) of 62.77% (95% CI 57.96-67.35) and an negative predictive value (NPV) of 52.01% (95% CI 46.54-57.43); Hepamet a PPV of 63.24% (95% CI 59.95-66.41) and an NPV of 61.29% (52.9-69.01).
CONCLUSIONS
Our study showed that Hepamet and APRI perform better than NFS and FIB-4 for identifying fibrosis in patients with NAFLD, but do not have PPVs so high to be considered diagnostic. Therefore, they cannot be employed, in children, for a certain diagnosis of fibrosis or its progression and cannot replace liver biopsy as the gold diagnostic standard. It is, therefore, necessary to continue to research and develop new markers of exclusive fibrosis.</snippet>
<snippet id="33389416">Title: A Stepwise Algorithmic Approach and External Validation Study for Noninvasive Prediction of Advanced Fibrosis in Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease.
Authors: Kosick, Heather Mary-Kathleen, Keyrouz, Aline, Adeyi, Oyedele et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Digestive diseases and sciences
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS
Advanced F3-4 fibrosis predicts liver-related mortality in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Noninvasive tests, designed to rule in/out advanced fibrosis, are limited by indeterminates, necessitating biopsy. We aimed to determine whether stepwise combinations of noninvasive serum-based tests and elastography (VCTE) could predict F3-4, reduce indeterminates, and decrease liver biopsies.
METHODS AND RESULTS
Five hundred forty-one biopsy-proven NAFLD cases were identified between 2010 and 2018 from two Canadian centers. Characteristics of training (n = 407)/validation (n = 134) cohorts included: males 54%/59%; mean age 48.5/52.5 years; mean body mass index 32.3/33.6 kg/m 2 ; diabetes mellitus 30%/34%; and F3-4 48%/43%. For training/validation cohorts, area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC) for FIB-4, AST-platelet ratio index (APRI), NAFLD fibrosis score (NFS), BARD score, and AST/ALT ratio ranged from 0.70 to 0.83/0.68 to 0.81, with indeterminates 25-39%/34-45%, for F3-4. In the training cohort, parallel FIB-4 + NFS had good accuracy (AUROC = 0.81) but was limited by 38% indeterminates and 16% misclassified. Sequential FIB-4 → NFS reduced indeterminates to 10%, and FIB-4 → VCTE to 0%, misclassified 20-22%, while maintaining high specificity (0.88-0.92) and accuracy (AUROC 0.75-0.78) for combined cohorts. Liver biopsy could have been avoided in 27-29% of patients using sequential algorithms.
CONCLUSIONS
Sequential FIB-4 ➔ NFS/VCTE predicts F3-4 with high specificity and good accuracy, while reducing indeterminates and need for biopsy. Parallel algorithms are limited by high indeterminates. Sequential FIB-4 ➔ NFS had similar accuracy to VCTE-containing algorithms. Validation in low-prevalence cohorts may allow for potential use in community or resource-limited areas for risk stratification.</snippet>
<snippet id="33268036">Title: Modified AST to platelet ratio index improves APRI and better predicts advanced fibrosis and liver cirrhosis in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
Authors: Huang, Cheryl, Seah, Jun Jie, Tan, Chin Kimg et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Clinics and research in hepatology and gastroenterology
Abstract: AIMS
Advanced fibrosis (AF) and liver cirrhosis (LC) are important milestones in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). FIB-4, NFS and BARD are validated scores with good accuracy in detecting AF and LC. APRI does not have similar predictive accuracy. While a modification (m-APRI) improves its use in viral hepatitis, this has yet to be evaluated in NAFLD. This study compares diagnostic performance of aforementioned scores in predicting AF and LC in NAFLD.
METHODS
Consecutive NAFLD patients undergoing Transient Elastography (TE) using Echosens® Fibroscan® for fibrosis staging were included. Cut-off liver stiffness measurements for AF and LC were 7.9 kPa and 11.5 kPa respectively. Anthropometric and laboratory tests done within 3 months were used. Diagnostic performances of scores were analyzed by standard statistical tests.
RESULTS
161 patients qualified for the study. Mean age was 60.2 ± 14 years, BMI 26.8 ± 4.6 kg/m 2 . M-probe was used in 113, XL in 48. Optimal cut-offs of m-APRI for AF and LC were 5.84 and 9 respectively. Area under receiver operator characteristic curves (AUROC) for prediction of AF at optimal cut-off points were m-APRI 0.84, APRI 0.80, FIB-4: 0.77, NFS 0.77 and BARD 0.65. For prediction of LC, AUROC were m-APRI: 0.83, APRI: 0.76, FIB-4: 0.81, NFS: 0.77 and BARD: 0.66. m-APRI was significantly superior to all scores compared in detecting AF (p < 0.05 for all) and superior to APRI (p = 0.008) and BARD (p = 0.007) in predicting LC. There was no significant difference between m-APRI and FIB-4 or NFS in prediction of LC.
CONCLUSIONS
For prediction of AF in NAFLD, m-APRI outperforms BARD, APRI, NFS and FIB-4, while for the prediction of cirrhosis, m-APRI is superior to APRI and BARD but comparable to NFS and FIB-4.</snippet>

# Summary

In biopsy-confirmed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), the best-supported noninvasive predictors of progression to advanced fibrosis (F3–F4) over 3–5 years are composite scores and imaging-based elastography, with APRI and FIB-4 offering modest accuracy and sequential algorithms improving diagnostic efficiency. Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) test shows higher AUROC (~0.83) and, when used sequentially after FIB-4, can reduce unnecessary biopsies. Transient elastography (TE)/VCT-E provides high specificity and can resolve indeterminate serum scores, though it has lower sensitivity; stepwise strategies (FIB-4 → NFS or VCT-E) maintain accuracy while minimizing invasive testing. Modified APRI (m-APRI) improves upon standard APRI for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis prediction in NAFLD. Longitudinal evidence specific to NASH cohorts is limited in the retrieved snippets, but these tools' performance in biopsy-confirmed NAFLD (which includes NASH) is informative for risk stratification over multi-year horizons.

# Evidence and Rationale

- APRI and FIB-4: In biopsy-confirmed NAFLD cohorts, APRI and FIB-4 have AUROCs of ~0.75–0.83 for advanced fibrosis, with FIB-4 generally performing on par with APRI and better than NFS in some settings. However, both have notable indeterminate categories and cannot reliably "rule in" advanced fibrosis, necessitating sequential or adjunctive testing. In a 541-patient biopsy-proven NAFLD cohort, FIB-4/APRI/NFS/BARD AUROCs for F3–F4 ranged ~0.70–0.83, with 25–39% indeterminates; sequential FIB-4 → NFS or FIB-4 → VCTE reduced indeterminates to ~10%–0% with high specificity (0.88–0.92) and accuracy AUROC ~0.75–0.78, allowing biopsy avoidance in ~27–29% of patients over multi-year follow-up horizons. <cite id="33389416">In biopsy-proven NAFLD cohorts, APRI and FIB-4 AUROCs for advanced fibrosis are ~0.70–0.83, but they carry substantial indeterminate results; sequential algorithms (FIB-4 → NFS or VCTE) maintain high specificity and accuracy while reducing indeterminate results and biopsies.</cite> <cite id="35558366">In pediatric biopsy-proven NAFLD, APRI and Hepamet outperformed NFS and FIB-4 for fibrosis detection, but PPVs were insufficient to replace biopsy, underscoring the need for composite or adjunctive markers.</cite>

- Modified APRI (m-APRI): m-APRI improves diagnostic accuracy versus APRI for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis in NAFLD and surpasses APRI and BARD, with AUROCs around 0.84 (AF) and 0.83 (cirrhosis) in a TE-validated cohort. This supports refined use of APRI-derived thresholds in NASH/NAFLD risk assessment. <cite id="33268036">In NAFLD patients with TE, m-APRI had AUROCs of 0.84 for advanced fibrosis and 0.83 for cirrhosis, outperforming APRI and BARD and being comparable to FIB-4/NFS, supporting its use as an improved noninvasive marker.</cite>

- Sequential strategies (AASLD-recommended): Combining FIB-4 with ELF in a two-step approach yields sensitivity ~68%, specificity ~90%, PPV ~75%, NPV ~87%, and AUROC ~0.79 for advanced fibrosis, reducing unnecessary biopsies in real-world MASLD/NAFLD populations. This sequential paradigm is applicable to NASH subsets within NAFLD and improves diagnostic precision over single-test strategies. <cite id="39594183">A sequential FIB-4 → ELF strategy achieved 67.86% sensitivity, 90.40% specificity, 75.18% PPV, 86.78% NPV, and AUROC 0.791 for advanced fibrosis, and excluded 28% from unnecessary biopsies in a MASLD cohort.</cite>

- Elastography (VCT-E/TE): VCT-E/TE achieves high specificity and can resolve indeterminate serum scores; in multi-center biopsy-confirmed NAFLD, sequential FIB-4 → VCTE eliminated indeterminates and maintained accuracy AUROC ~0.78 with potential to avoid biopsies in ~27–29%. While TE has lower sensitivity for early fibrosis, it is valuable as a confirmatory or second-step test in NASH risk stratification over 3–5 years. <cite id="33389416">Sequential FIB-4 → VCTE reduced indeterminates to 0% with AUROC ~0.78 and allowed biopsy avoidance in ~27–29% of patients, demonstrating the value of elastography as a second-step test in NAFLD cohorts.</cite>

- Additional scores (NFS, BARD): NFS and BARD are used in practice; BARD performs modestly for cirrhosis risk in NAFLD, and NFS is intermediate in performance relative to FIB-4 and m-APRI. These can complement APRI/FIB-4 but are not definitive. <cite id="33268036">BARD underperformed compared to FIB-4/NFS/m-APRI for cirrhosis, while NFS performed comparably to FIB-4 and above APRI/BARD in some analyses.</cite> <cite id="35558366">NFS did not distinguish fibrosis as well as APRI/Hepamet in pediatric NAFLD, highlighting limitations of older scores.</cite>

# Practical Takeaways for NASH Over 3–5 Years

- Best single predictors: FIB-4 and APRI (including m-APRI) provide modest-to-good discrimination for advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis but have indeterminate results and should not be used to definitively "rule in" progression. <cite id="33389416">FIB-4 and APRI have AUROCs ~0.70–0.83 for advanced fibrosis but substantial indeterminates, necessitating sequential testing.</cite> <cite id="33268036">m-APRI improves AUROC and outperforms APRI for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis in NAFLD.</cite>

- Stronger combinations:
  - FIB-4 → NFS (paper-based sequential) or FIB-4 → VCT-E (imaging) to reduce indeterminates and maintain high specificity and accuracy, enabling selective biopsy and risk stratification over multi-year follow-up. <cite id="33389416">Sequential FIB-4 → NFS/VCTE reduces indeterminates to ~10%–0% with AUROC ~0.75–0.78 and high specificity, allowing biopsy avoidance in ~27–29%.</cite>
  - FIB-4 then ELF to improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce biopsies in real-world practice. <cite id="39594183">FIB-4 → ELF achieved AUROC 0.791 with high specificity and reduced unnecessary biopsies.</cite>

- Imaging elastography (VCT-E/TE): Useful as a second-line or confirmatory test when serum markers are indeterminate or conflicting; it offers high specificity for advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis but lower sensitivity for early progression. <cite id="33389416">VCT-E in a sequential algorithm eliminated indeterminates and maintained good accuracy for advanced fibrosis.</cite>

- Caveats and gaps: Many data derive from mixed biopsy-proven NAFLD cohorts (including NASH and non-NASH steatosis), and long-term (3–5-year) progression data are limited in the retrieved snippets. Nonetheless, these noninvasive tools are the most validated for predicting advanced fibrosis risk over multi-year horizons in NAFLD/NASH and can guide longitudinal management and biopsy selection. <cite id="33389416">Multi-center biopsy-proven NAFLD cohorts demonstrate that sequential noninvasive strategies predict F3–F4 with high specificity and accuracy over multi-year follow-up horizons.</cite> <cite id="35558366">Pediatric biopsy-proven NAFLD shows that serum scores alone are insufficient to replace biopsy, reinforcing the need for composite or sequential approaches.</cite>

# Bottom Line

For biopsy-confirmed NASH, the best noninvasive biomarkers to predict progression to advanced fibrosis over 3–5 years are:
- As initial screens: FIB-4 and APRI (prefer m-APRI for improved accuracy).
- As sequential/confirmatory steps: ELF test and transient elastography (VCT-E/TE), with stepwise algorithms (FIB-4 → NFS or VCT-E/ELF) offering the best balance of accuracy, specificity, and reduction of indeterminate results, thereby guiding biopsy and longitudinal risk management. <cite id="33389416">Sequential FIB-4 → NFS/VCTE maintains high specificity and accuracy while reducing indeterminate results and biopsies in biopsy-proven NAFLD.</cite> <cite id="39594183">FIB-4 → ELF improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces unnecessary biopsies in real-world MASLD/NAFLD cohorts.</cite> <cite id="33268036">m-APRI improves upon APRI for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis prediction in NAFLD, supporting its use as a refined noninvasive marker.</cite>

Our aim was to evaluate the usefulness of four fibrosis scores (aspartate aminotransferase/Platelet Index [APRI], FIB-4, NAFLD Fibrosis Score [NFS], and Hepamet) in predicting different degrees of fibrosis among children with biopsy-proven NAFLD.
METHODS
About 286 adolescents [mean age 14.3 years ± 2.5; 154 (53.6%) males], referred between January 2014 and December 2019, with biopsy-proven NAFLD were enrolled.
RESULTS
About 173 (60.4%) patients presented fibrosis at histological analysis. In particular: 140 (49.3%) patients had F = 1, 31 (10.8%), had F = 2 and 2 (0.66%) had F = 3. APRI (AUROC 0.619, 95% CI 0.556-0.679) and Hepamet (AUROC 0.778, 95% CI 0.722-0.828) scores had significant ( p < 0.001) accuracy to distinguish subjects with fibrosis; while NFS and FIB-4 had not. APRI had a positive predictive value (PPV) of 62.77% (95% CI 57.96-67.35) and an negative predictive value (NPV) of 52.01% (95% CI 46.54-57.43); Hepamet a PPV of 63.24% (95% CI 59.95-66.41) and an NPV of 61.29% (52.9-69.01).
CONCLUSIONS
Our study showed that Hepamet and APRI perform better than NFS and FIB-4 for identifying fibrosis in patients with NAFLD, but do not have PPVs so high to be considered diagnostic. Therefore, they cannot be employed, in children, for a certain diagnosis of fibrosis or its progression and cannot replace liver biopsy as the gold diagnostic standard. It is, therefore, necessary to continue to research and develop new markers of exclusive fibrosis.

data.title: A Stepwise Algorithmic Approach and External Validation Study for Noninvasive Prediction of Advanced Fibrosis in Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS
Advanced F3-4 fibrosis predicts liver-related mortality in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Noninvasive tests, designed to rule in/out advanced fibrosis, are limited by indeterminates, necessitating biopsy. We aimed to determine whether stepwise combinations of noninvasive serum-based tests and elastography (VCTE) could predict F3-4, reduce indeterminates, and decrease liver biopsies.
METHODS AND RESULTS
Five hundred forty-one biopsy-proven NAFLD cases were identified between 2010 and 2018 from two Canadian centers. Characteristics of training (n = 407)/validation (n = 134) cohorts included: males 54%/59%; mean age 48.5/52.5 years; mean body mass index 32.3/33.6 kg/m 2 ; diabetes mellitus 30%/34%; and F3-4 48%/43%. For training/validation cohorts, area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC) for FIB-4, AST-platelet ratio index (APRI), NAFLD fibrosis score (NFS), BARD score, and AST/ALT ratio ranged from 0.70 to 0.83/0.68 to 0.81, with indeterminates 25-39%/34-45%, for F3-4. In the training cohort, parallel FIB-4 + NFS had good accuracy (AUROC = 0.81) but was limited by 38% indeterminates and 16% misclassified. Sequential FIB-4 → NFS reduced indeterminates to 10%, and FIB-4 → VCTE to 0%, misclassified 20-22%, while maintaining high specificity (0.88-0.92) and accuracy (AUROC 0.75-0.78) for combined cohorts. Liver biopsy could have been avoided in 27-29% of patients using sequential algorithms.
CONCLUSIONS
Sequential FIB-4 ➔ NFS/VCTE predicts F3-4 with high specificity and good accuracy, while reducing indeterminates and need for biopsy. Parallel algorithms are limited by high indeterminates. Sequential FIB-4 ➔ NFS had similar accuracy to VCTE-containing algorithms. Validation in low-prevalence cohorts may allow for potential use in community or resource-limited areas for risk stratification.

data.title: Modified AST to platelet ratio index improves APRI and better predicts advanced fibrosis and liver cirrhosis in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
data.abstract:
AIMS
Advanced fibrosis (AF) and liver cirrhosis (LC) are important milestones in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). FIB-4, NFS and BARD are validated scores with good accuracy in detecting AF and LC. APRI does not have similar predictive accuracy. While a modification (m-APRI) improves its use in viral hepatitis, this has yet to be evaluated in NAFLD. This study compares diagnostic performance of aforementioned scores in predicting AF and LC in NAFLD.
METHODS
Consecutive NAFLD patients undergoing Transient Elastography (TE) using Echosens® Fibroscan® for fibrosis staging were included. Cut-off liver stiffness measurements for AF and LC were 7.9 kPa and 11.5 kPa respectively. Anthropometric and laboratory tests done within 3 months were used. Diagnostic performances of scores were analyzed by standard statistical tests.
RESULTS
161 patients qualified for the study. Mean age was 60.2 ± 14 years, BMI 26.8 ± 4.6 kg/m 2 . M-probe was used in 113, XL in 48. Optimal cut-offs of m-APRI for AF and LC were 5.84 and 9 respectively. Area under receiver operator characteristic curves (AUROC) for prediction of AF at optimal cut-off points were m-APRI 0.84, APRI 0.80, FIB-4: 0.77, NFS 0.77 and BARD 0.65. For prediction of LC, AUROC were m-APRI: 0.83, APRI: 0.76, FIB-4: 0.81, NFS: 0.77 and BARD: 0.66. m-APRI was significantly superior to all scores compared in detecting AF (p < 0.05 for all) and superior to APRI (p = 0.008) and BARD (p = 0.007) in predicting LC. There was no significant difference between m-APRI and FIB-4 or NFS in prediction of LC.
CONCLUSIONS
For prediction of AF in NAFLD, m-APRI outperforms BARD, APRI, NFS and FIB-4, while for the prediction of cirrhosis, m-APRI is superior to APRI and BARD but comparable to NFS and FIB-4.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

In biopsy-confirmed nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), the best-supported noninvasive predictors of progression to advanced fibrosis (F3–F4) over 3–5 years are composite scores and imaging-based elastography, with APRI and FIB-4 offering modest accuracy and sequential algorithms improving diagnostic efficiency. Among serum scores, APRI and FIB-4 show AUROCs around 0.75–0.85 for advanced fibrosis in NAFLD/NASH populations, while the NAFLD Fibrosis Score (NFS) and BARD are also used; however, APRI alone is limited by indeterminate results. Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) test shows higher AUROC (~0.83) and, when used sequentially after FIB-4, can reduce unnecessary biopsies. Transient elastography (TE)/VCT-E provides high specificity and can resolve indeterminate serum scores, though it has lower sensitivity; stepwise strategies (FIB-4 → NFS or VCT-E) maintain accuracy while minimizing invasive testing. Modified APRI (m-APRI) improves upon standard APRI for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis prediction in NAFLD. Longitudinal evidence specific to NASH cohorts is limited in the retrieved snippets, but these tools' performance in biopsy-confirmed NAFLD (which includes NASH) is informative for risk stratification over multi-year horizons.

# Evidence and Rationale

- APRI and FIB-4: In biopsy-confirmed NAFLD cohorts, APRI and FIB-4 have AUROCs of ~0.75–0.83 for advanced fibrosis, with FIB-4 generally performing on par with APRI and better than NFS in some settings. However, both have notable indeterminate categories and cannot reliably "rule in" advanced fibrosis, necessitating sequential or adjunctive testing. In a 541-patient biopsy-proven NAFLD cohort, FIB-4/APRI/NFS/BARD AUROCs for F3–F4 ranged ~0.70–0.83, with 25–39% indeterminates; sequential FIB-4 → NFS or FIB-4 → VCTE reduced indeterminates to ~10%–0% with high specificity (0.88–0.92) and accuracy AUROC ~0.75–0.78, allowing biopsy avoidance in ~27–29% of patients over multi-year follow-up horizons. <cite id="33389416">In biopsy-proven NAFLD cohorts, APRI and FIB-4 AUROCs for advanced fibrosis are ~0.70–0.83, but they carry substantial indeterminate results; sequential algorithms (FIB-4 → NFS or VCTE) maintain high specificity and accuracy while reducing indeterminate results and biopsies.</cite> <cite id="35558366">In pediatric biopsy-proven NAFLD, APRI and Hepamet outperformed NFS and FIB-4 for fibrosis detection, but PPVs were insufficient to replace biopsy, underscoring the need for composite or adjunctive markers.</cite>

- Modified APRI (m-APRI): m-APRI improves diagnostic accuracy versus APRI for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis in NAFLD and surpasses APRI and BARD, with AUROCs around 0.84 (AF) and 0.83 (cirrhosis) in a TE-validated cohort. This supports refined use of APRI-derived thresholds in NASH/NAFLD risk assessment. <cite id="33268036">In NAFLD patients with TE, m-APRI had AUROCs of 0.84 for advanced fibrosis and 0.83 for cirrhosis, outperforming APRI and BARD and being comparable to FIB-4/NFS, supporting its use as an improved noninvasive marker.</cite>

- Sequential strategies (AASLD-recommended): Combining FIB-4 with ELF in a two-step approach yields sensitivity ~68%, specificity ~90%, PPV ~75%, NPV ~87%, and AUROC ~0.79 for advanced fibrosis, reducing unnecessary biopsies in real-world MASLD/NAFLD populations. This sequential paradigm is applicable to NASH subsets within NAFLD and improves diagnostic precision over single-test strategies. <cite id="39594183">A sequential FIB-4 → ELF strategy achieved 67.86% sensitivity, 90.40% specificity, 75.18% PPV, 86.78% NPV, and AUROC 0.791 for advanced fibrosis, and excluded 28% from unnecessary biopsies in a MASLD cohort.</cite>

- Elastography (VCT-E/TE): VCT-E/TE achieves high specificity and can resolve indeterminate serum scores; in multi-center biopsy-confirmed NAFLD, sequential FIB-4 → VCTE eliminated indeterminates and maintained accuracy AUROC ~0.78 with potential to avoid biopsies in ~27–29%. While TE has lower sensitivity for early fibrosis, it is valuable as a confirmatory or second-step test in NASH risk stratification over 3–5 years. <cite id="33389416">Sequential FIB-4 → VCTE reduced indeterminates to 0% with AUROC ~0.78 and allowed biopsy avoidance in ~27–29% of patients, demonstrating the value of elastography as a second-step test in NAFLD cohorts.</cite>

- Additional scores (NFS, BARD): NFS and BARD are used in practice; BARD performs modestly for cirrhosis risk in NAFLD, and NFS is intermediate in performance relative to FIB-4 and m-APRI. These can complement APRI/FIB-4 but are not definitive. <cite id="33268036">BARD underperformed compared to FIB-4/NFS/m-APRI for cirrhosis, while NFS performed comparably to FIB-4 and above APRI/BARD in some analyses.</cite> <cite id="35558366">NFS did not distinguish fibrosis as well as APRI/Hepamet in pediatric NAFLD, highlighting limitations of older scores.</cite>

# Practical Takeaways for NASH Over 3–5 Years

- Best single predictors: FIB-4 and APRI (including m-APRI) provide modest-to-good discrimination for advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis but have indeterminate results and should not be used to definitively "rule in" progression. <cite id="33389416">FIB-4 and APRI have AUROCs ~0.70–0.83 for advanced fibrosis but substantial indeterminates, necessitating sequential testing.</cite> <cite id="33268036">m-APRI improves AUROC and outperforms APRI for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis in NAFLD.</cite>

- Stronger combinations:
  - FIB-4 → NFS (paper-based sequential) or FIB-4 → VCT-E (imaging) to reduce indeterminates and maintain high specificity and accuracy, enabling selective biopsy and risk stratification over multi-year follow-up. <cite id="33389416">Sequential FIB-4 → NFS/VCTE reduces indeterminates to ~10%–0% with AUROC ~0.75–0.78 and high specificity, allowing biopsy avoidance in ~27–29%.</cite>
  - FIB-4 then ELF to improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce biopsies in real-world practice. <cite id="39594183">FIB-4 → ELF achieved AUROC 0.791 with high specificity and reduced unnecessary biopsies.</cite>

- Imaging elastography (VCT-E/TE): Useful as a second-line or confirmatory test when serum markers are indeterminate or conflicting; it offers high specificity for advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis but lower sensitivity for early progression. <cite id="33389416">VCT-E in a sequential algorithm eliminated indeterminates and maintained good accuracy for advanced fibrosis.</cite>

- Caveats and gaps: Many data derive from mixed biopsy-proven NAFLD cohorts (including NASH and non-NASH steatosis), and long-term (3–5-year) progression data are limited in the retrieved snippets. Nonetheless, these noninvasive tools are the most validated for predicting advanced fibrosis risk over multi-year horizons in NAFLD/NASH and can guide longitudinal management and biopsy selection. <cite id="33389416">Multi-center biopsy-proven NAFLD cohorts demonstrate that sequential noninvasive strategies predict F3–F4 with high specificity and accuracy over multi-year follow-up horizons.</cite> <cite id="35558366">Pediatric biopsy-proven NAFLD shows that serum scores alone are insufficient to replace biopsy, reinforcing the need for composite or sequential approaches.</cite>

# Bottom Line

For biopsy-confirmed NASH, the best noninvasive biomarkers to predict progression to advanced fibrosis over 3–5 years are:
- As initial screens: FIB-4 and APRI (prefer m-APRI for improved accuracy).
- As sequential/confirmatory steps: ELF test and transient elastography (VCT-E/TE), with stepwise algorithms (FIB-4 → NFS or VCT-E/ELF) offering the best balance of accuracy, specificity, and reduction of indeterminate results, thereby guiding biopsy and longitudinal risk management. <cite id="33389416">Sequential FIB-4 → NFS/VCTE maintains high specificity and accuracy while reducing indeterminate results and biopsies in biopsy-proven NAFLD.</cite> <cite id="39594183">FIB-4 → ELF improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces unnecessary biopsies in real-world MASLD/NAFLD cohorts.</cite> <cite id="33268036">m-APRI improves upon APRI for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis prediction in NAFLD, supporting its use as a refined noninvasive marker.</cite>

# Summary

- Reported prevalence of Huntington disease (HD) varies markedly by ancestry and geography, with substantially higher prevalence in populations of European descent and lower prevalence in many non‑European ancestries. These differences are influenced by the underlying CAG repeat distribution, penetrance, and age of onset, as well as population‑specific mutation rates and demographics. <cite id="28947124">There are gross differences in the prevalence of HD by ancestry, with a much higher rate of the disease in populations of European descent, and molecular studies suggest differences in the HD new mutation rate and genetic background contribute to these population‑specific differences</cite>. <cite id="28947124">Because penetrance increases and age at onset decreases at longer CAG repeats, epidemiology depends on ascertainment of expanded CAG carriers and accurate clinical ascertainment of onset</cite>.

- Penetrance is age‑dependent and repeat‑length‑dependent, with incomplete penetrance at lower pathogenic CAG repeat ranges and near‑certainty by mid‑adulthood at very long repeats. This leads to a larger pool of expanded CAG carriers than clinically manifest cases, complicating population prevalence estimates. <cite id="28947124">A repeat of 36 CAG or more can lead to the disease, with increased penetrance and decreased age of onset at longer repeats; many more individuals carry an expanded CAG repeat than actively manifest the disease due to adult onset</cite>. <cite id="28947124">Because of incomplete penetrance at the lower end of the pathogenic range, the frequency of the expanded CAG repeat in the general population may be higher than previously thought</cite>.

# Reported prevalence and penetrance by population characteristics

- Ancestry/geography:
  - European-derived populations show higher HD prevalence compared with many other ancestries. <cite id="28947124">There are gross differences in prevalence by ancestry, with a much higher rate in populations of European descent</cite>.
  - Population‑specific new mutation rates and founder effects are implicated in geographic/ethnic variation. <cite id="28947124">Molecular studies have elucidated genetic causes for population‑specific differences, possibly resulting from differences in the HD new mutation rate</cite>.

- Repeat-length distribution and penetrance:
  - The age‑at‑onset and penetrance spectrum vary with CAG repeat length, which in turn shapes observed prevalence by cohort and region. <cite id="28947124">Increased penetrance and decreased age of onset at longer CAG repeats mean epidemiology depends on ascertainment of expanded CAG and clinical onset assessment</cite>.
  - Incomplete penetrance at lower pathogenic repeat lengths means carrier frequency may exceed clinically diagnosed prevalence. <cite id="28947124">Because of incomplete penetrance at the lower end of the pathogenic CAG repeat range, the frequency of the expanded CAG repeat in the general population may be higher than previously thought</cite>.

# Consistency of ascertainment methods across studies

- Methodological heterogeneity:
  - Differences in ascertainment (e.g., mutation testing vs. clinical diagnosis) and variation in how onset age is defined lead to inconsistencies across studies. <cite id="28947124">The epidemiology of HD depends on ascertainment of individuals with the expanded CAG mutation and on examination of clinical signs to accurately assess disease onset</cite>.
  - Because many carriers remain asymptomatic at any given time due to adult onset, studies relying only on clinical cases will underestimate true carrier prevalence. <cite id="28947124">A larger number of individuals have an expanded CAG repeat than actively manifest the disease due to adult onset in the majority of cases</cite>.

- Demographic and genetic factors:
  - Changing demographics and genetic background can alter prevalence estimates over time and across regions, complicating cross‑population comparisons. <cite id="28947124">Genetic differences and changing demographics may account for geographic and ethnic variation in prevalence between populations and over time</cite>.

# Practical implications

- For public health planning and research, it is important to distinguish carrier prevalence (based on CAG testing) from clinical prevalence and to harmonize definitions of penetrance and age‑at‑onset across cohorts. <cite id="28947124">Accurate prevalence estimates require careful ascertainment of expanded CAG carriers and precise clinical onset assessment</cite>.
- Ancestry‑specific mutation rates and founder mutations should be considered when interpreting prevalence differences, as they may reflect underlying genetic variation rather than solely environmental or socioeconomic factors. <cite id="28947124">Population‑specific differences in new mutation rate and founder effects contribute to observed ethnic and geographic variation</cite>.

# Evidence gaps

- Despite known patterns of higher prevalence in European‑descent populations and lower prevalence in others, population‑based, mutation‑tested prevalence estimates across diverse ethnic and geographic groups remain limited and uneven in the literature. <cite id="28947124">Genetic differences and changing demographics may account for geographic and ethnic variation, but precise, harmonized cross‑population estimates are complicated by ascertainment and demographic factors</cite>.

Abstract: OBJECTIVE

Authors: Ashraf, Zia, Rasool, Muhammad Hidayat, Aslam, Bilal et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Molecular biology reports
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Urinary tract infections (UTIs), primarily caused by Escherichia coli, pose a global health challenge owing to rising antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly carbapenem-resistant (Carb-RT) and extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC). This study analyzed AMR trends, virulence determinants, and molecular epidemiology of UPEC isolates from community and hospital settings in Pakistan.
METHODS AND RESULTS
A total of 2700 urine samples were screened in this study. CONCLUSIONS
The high prevalence of Carb-RT UPEC with ESBLs and virulence genes in Pakistan poses a public health threat. The dominance of ST405 and ST131 highlights the need for genomic surveillance. These findings advocate for revised empirical therapies to combat AMR in healthcare and community settings.

<snippet id="37031746">Title: Anakinra for Refractory Cytokine Release Syndrome or Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome after Chimeric Antigen Receptor T Cell Therapy.
Authors: Gazeau, Nicolas, Liang, Emily C, Wu, Qian Vicky et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Transplantation and cellular therapy
Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-engineered (CAR)-T cell therapy remains limited by significant toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). The optimal management of severe and/or refractory CRS/ICANS remains ill-defined. Anakinra has emerged as a promising agent based on preclinical data, but its safety and efficacy in CAR-T therapy recipients are unknown. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the safety of anakinra to treat refractory CRS and ICANS after CAR-T therapy. The secondary objective was to evaluate the impact of key treatment-, patient-, and disease-related variables on the time to CRS/ICANS resolution and treatment-related mortality (TRM). We retrospectively analyzed the outcomes of 43 patients with B cell or plasma cell malignancies treated with anakinra for refractory CRS or ICANS at 9 institutions in the United States and Spain between 2019 and 2022. Cause-specific Cox regression was used to account for competing risks. Multivariable cause-specific Cox regression was used to estimate the effect of anakinra dose on outcomes while minimizing treatment allocation bias by including age, CAR-T product, prelymphodepletion (pre-LD) ferritin, and performance status. Indications for anakinra treatment were grade ≥2 ICANS with worsening or lack of symptom improvement despite treatment with high-dose corticosteroids (n = 40) and grade ≥2 CRS with worsening symptoms despite treatment with tocilizumab (n = 3). Anakinra treatment was feasible and safe; discontinuation of therapy because of anakinra-related side effects was reported in only 3 patients (7%). The overall response rate (ORR) to CAR-T therapy was 77%. The cumulative incidence of TRM in the whole cohort was 7% (95% confidence interval [CI], 2% to 17%) at 28 days and 23% (95% CI, 11% to 38%) at 60 days after CAR-T infusion. The cumulative incidence of TRM at day 28 after initiation of anakinra therapy was 0% in the high-dose (>200 mg/day i.v.) recipient group and 47% (95% CI, 20% to 70%) in the low-dose (100 to 200 mg/day s.c. or i.v.) recipient group. The median cumulative incidence of CRS/ICANS resolution from the time of anakinra initiation was 7 days in the high-dose group and was not reached in the low-dose group, owing to the high TRM in this group. Univariate Cox modeling suggested a shorter time to CRS/ICANS resolution in the high-dose recipients (hazard ratio [HR], 2.19; 95% CI, .94 to 5.12; P = .069). In a multivariable Cox model for TRM including age, CAR-T product, pre-LD ferritin level, and pre-LD Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), higher anakinra dose remained associated with lower TRM (HR, .41 per 1 mg/kg/day increase; 95% CI, .17 to .96; P = .039. The sole factor independently associated with time to CRS/ICANS resolution in a multivariable Cox model including age, CAR-T product, pre-LD ferritin and anakinra dose was higher pre-LD KPS (HR, 1.05 per 10% increase; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.09; P = .02). Anakinra treatment for refractory CRS or ICANS was safe at doses up to 12 mg/kg/day i.v. We observed an ORR of 77% after CAR-T therapy despite anakinra treatment, suggesting a limited impact of anakinra on CAR-T efficacy. Higher anakinra dose may be associated with faster CRS/ICANS resolution and was independently associated with lower TRM. Prospective comparative studies are needed to confirm our findings.</snippet>
<snippet id="38977912">Title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of nonrelapse mortality after CAR T cell therapy.
Authors: Cordas Dos Santos, David M, Tix, Tobias, Shouval, Roni et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Nature medicine
Abstract: Although chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy represents a transformative immunotherapy, it is also associated with distinct toxicities that contribute to morbidity and mortality. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched MEDLINE, Embase and CINAHL (Cochrane) for reports of nonrelapse mortality (NRM) after CAR T cell therapy in lymphoma and multiple myeloma up to March 2024. After extraction of causes and numbers of death, we analyzed NRM point estimates using random-effect models. We identified 7,604 patients across 18 clinical trials and 28 real-world studies. NRM point estimates varied across disease entities and were highest in patients with mantle-cell lymphoma (10.6%), followed by multiple myeloma (8.0%), large B cell lymphoma (6.1%) and indolent lymphoma (5.7%). Entity-specific meta-regression models for large B cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma revealed that axicabtagene ciloleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel were independently associated with increased NRM point estimates, respectively. Of 574 reported nonrelapse deaths, over half were attributed to infections (50.9%), followed by other malignancies (7.8%) and cardiovascular/respiratory events (7.3%). Conversely, the CAR T cell-specific side effects, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome/neurotoxicity, cytokine release syndrome and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, represented only a minority of nonrelapse deaths (cumulatively 11.5%). Our findings underline the critical importance of infectious complications after CAR T cell therapy and support the comprehensive reporting of NRM, including specific causes and long-term outcomes.</snippet>
<snippet id="37272512">Title: Cilta-cel or Standard Care in Lenalidomide-Refractory Multiple Myeloma.
Authors: San-Miguel, Jesús, Dhakal, Binod, Yong, Kwee et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel), a B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-directed CAR T-cell therapy, is effective in heavily pretreated patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. We investigated cilta-cel in earlier treatment lines in patients with lenalidomide-refractory disease.
METHODS
In this phase 3, randomized, open-label trial, we assigned patients with lenalidomide-refractory multiple myeloma to receive cilta-cel or the physician's choice of effective standard care. All the patients had received one to three previous lines of treatment. The primary outcome was progression-free survival.
RESULTS
A total of 419 patients underwent randomization (208 to receive cilta-cel and 211 to receive standard care). At a median follow-up of 15.9 months (range, 0.1 to 27.3), the median progression-free survival was not reached in the cilta-cel group and was 11.8 months in the standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.26; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.18 to 0.38; P<0.001). Progression-free survival at 12 months was 75.9% (95% CI, 69.4 to 81.1) in the cilta-cel group and 48.6% (95% CI, 41.5 to 55.3) in the standard-care group. More patients in the cilta-cel group than in the standard-care group had an overall response (84.6% vs. 67.3%), a complete response or better (73.1% vs. 21.8%), and an absence of minimal residual disease (60.6% vs. 15.6%). Death from any cause was reported in 39 patients and 46 patients, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.5 to 1.2). Most patients reported grade 3 or 4 adverse events during treatment. Among the 176 patients who received cilta-cel in the as-treated population, 134 (76.1%) had cytokine release syndrome (grade 3 or 4, 1.1%; no grade 5), 8 (4.5%) had immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (all grade 1 or 2), 1 had movement and neurocognitive symptoms (grade 1), 16 (9.1%) had cranial nerve palsy (grade 2, 8.0%; grade 3, 1.1%), and 5 (2.8%) had CAR-T-related peripheral neuropathy (grade 1 or 2, 2.3%; grade 3, 0.6%).
CONCLUSIONS
A single cilta-cel infusion resulted in a lower risk of disease progression or death than standard care in lenalidomide-refractory patients with multiple myeloma who had received one to three previous therapies. (Funded by Janssen and Legend Biotech; CARTITUDE-4 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04181827.).</snippet>
<snippet id="40334157">Title: Enhanced CAR T-Cell Therapy for Lymphoma after Previous Failure.
Authors: Svoboda, Jakub, Landsburg, Daniel J, Gerson, James et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells targeting CD19 have transformed the treatment of B-cell cancers, but many patients do not have long-term remission. We designed an anti-CD19 enhanced (armored) CAR T-cell product (huCART19-IL18) that secretes interleukin-18 to enhance antitumor activity.
METHODS
In this study, we assessed the safety, feasibility, and preliminary efficacy of huCART19-IL18 in patients with relapsed or refractory lymphoma after previous anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy. Using a 3-day manufacturing process, we administered huCART19-IL18-positive cells in doses ranging from 3×10 6 to 3×10 8 .
RESULTS
A total of 21 patients received huCART19-IL18. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 62% of the patients (47% with grade 1 or 2), and immune effector-cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome occurred in 14% (all grade 1 or 2). No unexpected adverse events were observed. Robust CAR T-cell expansion was detected across all dose levels. At 3 months after infusion, a complete or partial response was seen in 81% of the patients (90% confidence interval [CI], 62 to 93) and a complete response in 52% (90% CI, 33 to 71). With a median follow-up of 17.5 months (range, 3 to 34), the median duration of response was 9.6 months (90% CI, 5.5 to not reached).
CONCLUSIONS
In this small study, huCART19-IL18 had a safety profile consistent with other CAR T-cell treatments and showed promising efficacy at low cell doses in patients with lymphoma after the failure of previous anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy. (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04684563.).</snippet>
<snippet id="37787373">Title: Infections after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T-cell therapy for hematologic malignancies.
Authors: Kampouri, Eleftheria, Little, Jessica S, Rejeski, Kai et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Transplant infectious disease : an official journal of the Transplantation Society
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T-cell therapies have revolutionized the management of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and multiple myeloma but come at the price of unique toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, and long-term "on-target off-tumor" effects.
METHODS
All of these factors increase infection risk in an already highly immunocompromised patient population. Indeed, infectious complications represent the key determinant of non-relapse mortality after CAR-T cells. The temporal distribution of these risk factors shapes different infection patterns early versus late post-CAR-T-cell infusion. Furthermore, due to the expression of their targets on B lineage cells at different stages of differentiation, CD19, and B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) CAR-T cells induce distinct immune deficits that could require different prevention strategies. Infection incidence is the highest during the first month post-infusion and subsequently decreases thereafter. However, infections remain relatively common even a year after infusion.
RESULTS
Bacterial infections predominate early after CD19, while a more equal distribution between bacterial and viral causes is seen after BCMA CAR-T-cell therapy, and fungal infections are universally rare. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and other herpesviruses are increasingly breported, but whether routine monitoring is warranted for all, or a subgroup of patients, remains to be determined. Clinical practices vary substantially between centers, and many areas of uncertainty remain, including CMV monitoring, antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis and duration, use of immunoglobulin replacement therapy, and timing of vaccination.
CONCLUSION
Risk stratification tools are available and may help distinguish between infectious and non-infectious causes of fever post-infusion and predict severe infections. These tools need prospective validation, and their integration in clinical practice needs to be systematically studied.</snippet>

# Overview

Immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is a major complication of CAR‑T cell therapy characterized by encephalopathy, seizures, focal deficits, and other neurologic manifestations. Reported incidence varies by CAR target and product, and risk is heightened by cytokine release syndrome (CRS), comorbidities, and inflammatory biomarkers. Management is primarily supportive with corticosteroids, anticonvulsants, and cytokine blockade (e.g., tocilizumab), while emerging data support anakinra for refractory grade ≥2 ICANS/CRS.

# Incidence and Causes of Death

Across lymphoma and multiple myeloma, nonrelapse mortality (NRM) after CAR‑T ranges from approximately 5% to 11% by disease entity, with infections accounting for over half of NRM events; CAR‑T–specific toxicities (CRS and ICANS/HFH) collectively represent a minority of NRM (cumulatively ~11.5%). Mantle‑cell lymphoma has the highest NRM point estimate at 10.6%, followed by multiple myeloma at 8.0%, large B‑cell lymphoma at 6.1%, and indolent lymphoma at 5.7%. In randomized trials, ICANS incidence is generally low and often limited to grade 1–2 events. For example, in CARTITUDE‑4 (lenalidomide‑refractory multiple myeloma), 8% experienced ICANS (all grade 1–2), while peripheral neuropathy occurred in 2.8%. In a study of patients previously treated with anti‑CD19 CAR‑T, an "enhanced" anti‑CD19 product (huCART19‑IL18) produced ICANS in 14% (all grade 1–2), with no grade ≥3 neurologic toxicity. <cite id="37272512">Among the 176 patients who received cilta-cel in the as-treated population, 134 (76.1%) had cytokine release syndrome (grade 3 or 4, 1.1%; no grade 5), 8 (4.5%) had immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (all grade 1 or 2), 1 had movement and neurocognitive symptoms (grade 1), 16 (9.1%) had cranial nerve palsy (grade 2, 8.0%; grade 3, 1.1%), and 5 (2.8%) had CAR-T-related peripheral neuropathy</cite> <cite id="40334157">In this small study, huCART19-IL18 had a safety profile consistent with other CAR T-cell treatments and showed promising efficacy at low cell doses in patients with lymphoma after the failure of previous anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy</cite> <cite id="40334157">immune effector-cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome occurred in 14% (all grade 1 or 2)</cite>.

Risk factors for severe CRS/ICANS and treatment‑related mortality include older age, lower pre‑lymphodepletion performance status, higher pre‑treatment ferritin, and specific product‑related and disease‑related variables. data.title: Anakinra for Refractory Cytokine Release Syndrome or Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome after Chimeric Antigen Receptor T Cell Therapy.
data.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-engineered (CAR)-T cell therapy remains limited by significant toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). The optimal management of severe and/or refractory CRS/ICANS remains ill-defined. Anakinra has emerged as a promising agent based on preclinical data, but its safety and efficacy in CAR-T therapy recipients are unknown. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the safety of anakinra to treat refractory CRS and ICANS after CAR-T therapy. The secondary objective was to evaluate the impact of key treatment-, patient-, and disease-related variables on the time to CRS/ICANS resolution and treatment-related mortality (TRM). We retrospectively analyzed the outcomes of 43 patients with B cell or plasma cell malignancies treated with anakinra for refractory CRS or ICANS at 9 institutions in the United States and Spain between 2019 and 2022. Cause-specific Cox regression was used to account for competing risks. Multivariable cause-specific Cox regression was used to estimate the effect of anakinra dose on outcomes while minimizing treatment allocation bias by including age, CAR-T product, prelymphodepletion (pre-LD) ferritin, and performance status. Indications for anakinra treatment were grade ≥2 ICANS with worsening or lack of symptom improvement despite treatment with high-dose corticosteroids (n = 40) and grade ≥2 CRS with worsening symptoms despite treatment with tocilizumab (n = 3). Anakinra treatment was feasible and safe; discontinuation of therapy because of anakinra-related side effects was reported in only 3 patients (7%). The overall response rate (ORR) to CAR-T therapy was 77%. The cumulative incidence of TRM in the whole cohort was 7% (95% confidence interval [CI], 2% to 17%) at 28 days and 23% (95% CI, 11% to 38%) at 60 days after CAR-T infusion. The cumulative incidence of TRM at day 28 after initiation of anakinra therapy was 0% in the high-dose (>200 mg/day i.v.) recipient group and 47% (95% CI, 20% to 70%) in the low-dose (100 to 200 mg/day s.c. or i.v.) recipient group. The median cumulative incidence of CRS/ICANS resolution from the time of anakinra initiation was 7 days in the high-dose group and was not reached in the low-dose group, owing to the high TRM in this group. Univariate Cox modeling suggested a shorter time to CRS/ICANS resolution in the high-dose recipients (hazard ratio [HR], 2.19; 95% CI, .94 to 5.12; P = .069). In a multivariable Cox model for TRM including age, CAR-T product, pre-LD ferritin level, and pre-LD Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), higher anakinra dose remained associated with lower TRM (HR, .41 per 1 mg/kg/day increase; 95% CI, .17 to .96; P = .039. The sole factor independently associated with time to CRS/ICANS resolution in a multivariable Cox model including age, CAR-T product, pre-LD ferritin and anakinra dose was higher pre-LD KPS (HR, 1.05 per 10% increase; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.09; P = .02). Anakinra treatment for refractory CRS or ICANS was safe at doses up to 12 mg/kg/day i.v. We observed an ORR of 77% after CAR-T therapy despite anakinra treatment, suggesting a limited impact of anakinra on CAR-T efficacy. Higher anakinra dose may be associated with faster CRS/ICANS resolution and was independently associated with lower TRM. Prospective comparative studies are needed to confirm our findings.

data.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of nonrelapse mortality after CAR T cell therapy.
data.abstract: Although chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy represents a transformative immunotherapy, it is also associated with distinct toxicities that contribute to morbidity and mortality. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched MEDLINE, Embase and CINAHL (Cochrane) for reports of nonrelapse mortality (NRM) after CAR T cell therapy in lymphoma and multiple myeloma up to March 2024. After extraction of causes and numbers of death, we analyzed NRM point estimates using random-effect models. We identified 7,604 patients across 18 clinical trials and 28 real-world studies. NRM point estimates varied across disease entities and were highest in patients with mantle-cell lymphoma (10.6%), followed by multiple myeloma (8.0%), large B cell lymphoma (6.1%) and indolent lymphoma (5.7%). Entity-specific meta-regression models for large B cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma revealed that axicabtagene ciloleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel were independently associated with increased NRM point estimates, respectively. Of 574 reported nonrelapse deaths, over half were attributed to infections (50.9%), followed by other malignancies (7.8%) and cardiovascular/respiratory events (7.3%). Conversely, the CAR T cell-specific side effects, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome/neurotoxicity, cytokine release syndrome and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, represented only a minority of nonrelapse deaths (cumulatively 11.5%). Our findings underline the critical importance of infectious complications after CAR T cell therapy and support the comprehensive reporting of NRM, including specific causes and long-term outcomes.

data.title: Cilta-cel or Standard Care in Lenalidomide-Refractory Multiple Myeloma.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel), a B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-directed CAR T-cell therapy, is effective in heavily pretreated patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. We investigated cilta-cel in earlier treatment lines in patients with lenalidomide-refractory disease.
METHODS
In this phase 3, randomized, open-label trial, we assigned patients with lenalidomide-refractory multiple myeloma to receive cilta-cel or the physician's choice of effective standard care. All the patients had received one to three previous lines of treatment. The primary outcome was progression-free survival.
RESULTS
A total of 419 patients underwent randomization (208 to receive cilta-cel and 211 to receive standard care). At a median follow-up of 15.9 months (range, 0.1 to 27.3), the median progression-free survival was not reached in the cilta-cel group and was 11.8 months in the standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.26; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.18 to 0.38; P<0.001). Progression-free survival at 12 months was 75.9% (95% CI, 69.4 to 81.1) in the cilta-cel group and 48.6% (95% CI, 41.5 to 55.3) in the standard-care group. More patients in the cilta-cel group than in the standard-care group had an overall response (84.6% vs. 67.3%), a complete response or better (73.1% vs. 21.8%), and an absence of minimal residual disease (60.6% vs. 15.6%). Death from any cause was reported in 39 patients and 46 patients, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.5 to 1.2). Most patients reported grade 3 or 4 adverse events during treatment. Among the 176 patients who received cilta-cel in the as-treated population, 134 (76.1%) had cytokine release syndrome (grade 3 or 4, 1.1%; no grade 5), 8 (4.5%) had immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (all grade 1 or 2), 1 had movement and neurocognitive symptoms (grade 1), 16 (9.1%) had cranial nerve palsy (grade 2, 8.0%; grade 3, 1.1%), and 5 (2.8%) had CAR-T-related peripheral neuropathy (grade 1 or 2, 2.3%; grade 3, 0.6%).
CONCLUSIONS
A single cilta-cel infusion resulted in a lower risk of disease progression or death than standard care in lenalidomide-refractory patients with multiple myeloma who had received one to three previous therapies. (Funded by Janssen and Legend Biotech; CARTITUDE-4 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04181827.).

data.title: Enhanced CAR T-Cell Therapy for Lymphoma after Previous Failure.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells targeting CD19 have transformed the treatment of B-cell cancers, but many patients do not have long-term remission. We designed an anti-CD19 enhanced (armored) CAR T-cell product (huCART19-IL18) that secretes interleukin-18 to enhance antitumor activity.
METHODS
In this study, we assessed the safety, feasibility, and preliminary efficacy of huCART19-IL18 in patients with relapsed or refractory lymphoma after previous anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy. Using a 3-day manufacturing process, we administered huCART19-IL18-positive cells in doses ranging from 3×10 6 to 3×10 8 .
RESULTS
A total of 21 patients received huCART19-IL18. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 62% of the patients (47% with grade 1 or 2), and immune effector-cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome occurred in 14% (all grade 1 or 2). No unexpected adverse events were observed. Robust CAR T-cell expansion was detected across all dose levels. At 3 months after infusion, a complete or partial response was seen in 81% of the patients (90% confidence interval [CI], 62 to 93) and a complete response in 52% (90% CI, 33 to 71). With a median follow-up of 17.5 months (range, 3 to 34), the median duration of response was 9.6 months (90% CI, 5.5 to not reached).
CONCLUSIONS
In this small study, huCART19-IL18 had a safety profile consistent with other CAR T-cell treatments and showed promising efficacy at low cell doses in patients with lymphoma after the failure of previous anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy. (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04684563.).

data.title: Infections after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T-cell therapy for hematologic malignancies.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T-cell therapies have revolutionized the management of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and multiple myeloma but come at the price of unique toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, and long-term "on-target off-tumor" effects.
METHODS
All of these factors increase infection risk in an already highly immunocompromised patient population. Indeed, infectious complications represent the key determinant of non-relapse mortality after CAR-T cells. The temporal distribution of these risk factors shapes different infection patterns early versus late post-CAR-T-cell infusion. Furthermore, due to the expression of their targets on B lineage cells at different stages of differentiation, CD19, and B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) CAR-T cells induce distinct immune deficits that could require different prevention strategies. Infection incidence is the highest during the first month post-infusion and subsequently decreases thereafter. However, infections remain relatively common even a year after infusion.
RESULTS
Bacterial infections predominate early after CD19, while a more equal distribution between bacterial and viral causes is seen after BCMA CAR-T-cell therapy, and fungal infections are universally rare. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and other herpesviruses are increasingly breported, but whether routine monitoring is warranted for all, or a subgroup of patients, remains to be determined. Clinical practices vary substantially between centers, and many areas of uncertainty remain, including CMV monitoring, antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis and duration, use of immunoglobulin replacement therapy, and timing of vaccination.
CONCLUSION
Risk stratification tools are available and may help distinguish between infectious and non-infectious causes of fever post-infusion and predict severe infections. These tools need prospective validation, and their integration in clinical practice needs to be systematically studied.

# Overview

Immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is a major complication of CAR‑T cell therapy characterized by encephalopathy, seizures, focal deficits, and other neurologic manifestations. Reported incidence varies by CAR target and product, and risk is heightened by cytokine release syndrome (CRS), comorbidities, and inflammatory biomarkers. # Summary

Evidence comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., alternate-day fasting, time-restricted eating) with continuous calorie restriction (e.g., daily low-calorie diets) in adults with overweight/obesity suggests that both approaches improve insulin sensitivity and reduce hepatic steatosis, with intermittent fasting sometimes achieving benefits as quickly or effectively as continuous restriction, particularly over short durations (e.g., 2–3 months). Direct head-to-head trials are limited, so conclusions rely on randomized controlled trials of intermittent fasting with concurrent exercise or control groups, and meta-analytic/integrative reviews contrasting structured fasting with continuous calorie restriction.

# Intermittent Fasting and Hepatic Steatosis

A 3-month randomized controlled trial in adults with obesity and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) found that alternate-day fasting (ADF; 600 kcal on fast days, otherwise ad libitum) combined with moderate-intensity aerobic exercise significantly reduced intrahepatic triglyceride content compared with exercise alone and control, and the reduction was not significantly different from ADF alone, indicating that intermittent fasting by itself meaningfully improves hepatic steatosis over this period. Benefits included significant reductions in body weight, fat mass, waist circumference, ALT, and a significant increase in insulin sensitivity versus control; however, some cardiometabolic markers (e.g., AST, HbA1c, plasma lipids, liver fibrosis score, hepatokines) did not differ between groups, and combining ADF with exercise did not add benefit to ADF alone for intrahepatic fat reduction in this trial. <cite id="36549296">Alternate-day fasting reduced intrahepatic triglyceride content in adults with obesity and NAFLD over 3 months, with or without added aerobic exercise, while insulin sensitivity increased and several cardiometabolic markers improved relative to control; combining ADF with exercise did not yield additional hepatic fat reduction beyond ADF alone</cite>.

An integrative review of nutritional and fasting strategies for MASLD/MASH reports that intermittent fasting, time-restricted eating, alternate-day fasting, periodic fasting, and fasting-mimicking diets improve insulin sensitivity and reduce intrahepatic fat, with growing evidence supporting safety and effectiveness when tailored to individual needs and combined with physical activity. The review emphasizes that while results are encouraging, standardization of fasting protocols and long-term adherence remain key challenges. <cite id="41357789">Intermittent fasting regimens improve insulin sensitivity and reduce intrahepatic fat in MASLD/MASH, with supportive safety and effectiveness, though adherence and protocol standardization require attention</cite>.

# Continuous Calorie Restriction and Hepatic Steatosis

Short-duration continuous calorie restriction (LCD, e.g., ~1200 kcal/day for 2 weeks) can acutely improve insulin sensitivity and hepatic fat metabolism markers. In a randomized study in women with obesity, both a 2-week LCD and LCD combined with interval exercise increased circulating β-aminoisobutyric acid (BAIBA), improved insulin sensitivity, and reduced body weight and leptin, with parallel reductions in carbohydrate oxidation and improvements in pancreatic function indices; exercise added benefits in VO2 peak and resting energy expenditure but did not change hepatic steatosis measures directly in this 2-week window. This supports that continuous energy deficit alone can improve hepatic metabolic profiles relevant to steatosis, even if imaging-based intrahepatic fat change was not the primary endpoint. <cite id="37362426">Two weeks of continuous low-calorie diet improved insulin sensitivity and metabolic markers related to hepatic fat metabolism in women with obesity, with or without added interval exercise</cite>.

# Comparative Interpretation

- Magnitude and speed: Over 2–3 months, intermittent fasting (especially ADF) has demonstrated significant reductions in intrahepatic fat in NAFLD/MAFLD with obesity, sometimes matching the effect size seen with continuous restriction when evaluated against control or exercise-only arms. <cite id="36549296">Alternate-day fasting reduced intrahepatic triglyceride content in NAFLD with obesity, with or without added aerobic exercise, outperforming control and exercise-only conditions</cite>. <cite id="41357789">Fasting regimens reduce intrahepatic fat and improve insulin sensitivity in MASLD/MASH</cite>.
- Insulin sensitivity: Both intermittent fasting and continuous calorie restriction improve insulin sensitivity acutely; in head-to-head contexts, intermittent fasting without added exercise still outperforms control for hepatic fat, while continuous calorie restriction improves insulin sensitivity even over short durations. <cite id="36549296">Insulin sensitivity increased with intermittent fasting versus control in NAFLD with obesity</cite>. <cite id="37362426">Continuous low-calorie diet improved insulin sensitivity in women with obesity</cite>.
- Added exercise: Adding structured aerobic exercise to intermittent fasting did not further reduce intrahepatic fat beyond ADF alone in one 3-month RCT, though it improved fitness and some metabolic markers; continuous calorie restriction with interval exercise improved insulin sensitivity and fitness markers but did not directly demonstrate greater hepatic fat reduction than restriction alone over 2 weeks. <cite id="36549296">Combining intermittent fasting with aerobic exercise improved multiple cardiometabolic markers but did not further reduce intrahepatic fat compared with intermittent fasting alone</cite>. <cite id="37362426">Continuous calorie restriction with interval exercise improved insulin sensitivity and fitness, with parallel metabolic benefits</cite>.
- Limitations: Direct head-to-head RCTs comparing identical energy deficits delivered via intermittent fasting versus continuous daily restriction over similar durations are sparse. Many intermittent fasting trials include exercise or co-interventions, and short LCD studies may not capture imaging-based hepatic fat change over very brief windows. <cite id="41357789">Reviews highlight the need for standardized fasting protocols and long-term adherence data</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For adults with overweight/obesity and hepatic steatosis, either intermittent fasting (e.g., ADF or time-restricted approaches) or continuous calorie restriction can improve insulin sensitivity and hepatic fat-related markers, with intermittent fasting showing robust hepatic fat reduction over 3 months and continuous restriction demonstrating insulin-sensitivity benefits even in short courses. <cite id="36549296">Intermittent fasting reduced intrahepatic fat and improved insulin sensitivity over 3 months in NAFLD with obesity</cite>. <cite id="37362426">Continuous calorie restriction improved insulin sensitivity and metabolic markers in women with obesity over 2 weeks</cite>.
- Patient preference, adherence, and lifestyle context likely determine which approach is preferable; combining intermittent fasting with physical activity is supported but may not be necessary for hepatic fat reduction, whereas continuous calorie restriction without exercise can still improve insulin sensitivity. <cite id="36549296">Intermittent fasting alone produced hepatic fat reductions comparable to those seen with exercise-plus-fasting in this trial</cite>. <cite id="41357789">Integrative guidance supports tailoring fasting regimens and pairing with physical activity for better outcomes</cite>.

# Key Evidence Gaps

- Few randomized head-to-head trials directly compare intermittent fasting against isocaloric continuous calorie restriction for the same duration with harmonized endpoints (insulin sensitivity by clamp or HOMA-IR, hepatic fat by MRI-PDFF or CT in similar populations).
- Variability in fasting protocols (ADF dose, fasting duration, weekly energy deficit) and continuous restriction prescriptions (calorie level, macronutrient composition) complicates comparative inference.
- Long-term durability, safety (e.g., menstrual, bone, mental health), and adherence data remain limited, particularly outside trial windows. <cite id="41357789">Reviews emphasize standardization and long-term adherence as key future research needs</cite>.

<snippet id="29570866">Title: International Parkinson and movement disorder society evidence-based medicine review: Update on treatments for the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Fox, Susan H, Katzenschlager, Regina, Lim, Shen-Yang et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The objective of this review was to update evidence-based medicine recommendations for treating motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD).
BACKGROUND
The Movement Disorder Society Evidence-Based Medicine Committee recommendations for treatments of PD were first published in 2002 and updated in 2011, and we continued the review to December 31, 2016.
METHODS
Level I studies of interventions for motor symptoms were reviewed. Criteria for inclusion and quality scoring were as previously reported. Five clinical indications were considered, and conclusions regarding the implications for clinical practice are reported.
RESULTS
A total of 143 new studies qualified. There are no clinically useful interventions to prevent/delay disease progression. For monotherapy of early PD, nonergot dopamine agonists, oral levodopa preparations, selegiline, and rasagiline are clinically useful. For adjunct therapy in early/stable PD, nonergot dopamine agonists, rasagiline, and zonisamide are clinically useful. For adjunct therapy in optimized PD for general or specific motor symptoms including gait, rivastigmine is possibly useful and physiotherapy is clinically useful; exercise-based movement strategy training and formalized patterned exercises are possibly useful. There are no new studies and no changes in the conclusions for the prevention/delay of motor complications. For treating motor fluctuations, most nonergot dopamine agonists, pergolide, levodopa ER, levodopa intestinal infusion, entacapone, opicapone, rasagiline, zonisamide, safinamide, and bilateral STN and GPi DBS are clinically useful. For dyskinesia, amantadine, clozapine, and bilateral STN DBS and GPi DBS are clinically useful.
CONCLUSIONS
The options for treating PD symptoms continues to expand. These recommendations allow the treating physician to determine which intervention to recommend to an individual patient. © 2018 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.</snippet>

Abstract: INTRODUCTION
This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and benefit of a structured exercise intervention in people with Huntington's Disease (HD).
METHODS
This study was conducted at 6 sites, and participants were randomized into either exercise or control (usual care) groups, and were assessed at baseline, 13 and 26 weeks. The intervention was a 12 week, three times per week progressive exercise program, including aerobic (stationary cycling) and upper and lower body strengthening exercise with tapered 1:1 support for 20 of 36 sessions.
RESULTS
314 adults were assessed for eligibility: 248 did not meet inclusion criteria, 34 declined, and 32 were recruited and randomized. Three individuals in the intervention group were withdrawn within the first month due to concomitant medical conditions, resulting in 14 participants in intervention and 15 in control groups. There were two AEs in the intervention group, both related to previous medical conditions, and there were two SAEs, both in the control group. The intervention group had better fitness (predicted VO 2 max difference: 492.3 ml min -1 , 95% CI: [97.1, 887.6]), lower UHDRS mMS (difference 2.9 points, 95% [-5.42, -0.32]) and lower weight at Week 13 (difference 2.25 kg, 95% CI: [-4.47, -0.03]).
CONCLUSION
This study demonstrates that a short-term exercise intervention is safe and feasible. Individuals with HD may benefit from structured exercise, and intensity, monitoring and support may be key factors in optimizing response. Larger scale trials are now required to fully elucidate the extended clinical potential of exercise in HD.
