# Evidence in SLE and lupus nephritis

- Circulating NETs correlate with anti-dsDNA and disease activity. Reviews synthesize that accumulation of NETs in circulation correlates with anti-dsDNA antibody formation and SLE pathogenesis; impaired NET clearance due to anti-DNase autoantibodies or mutations in DNASE1L3 leads to NET accumulation and is associated with severe lupus-like syndromes and lupus nephritis. <cite id="34685647">Accumulation of NETs correlates with anti-dsDNA antibodies and is considered a causative factor for SLE; mutations in DNASE1/DNASE1L3 determine anti-DNA formation and are associated with severe lupus-like syndromes and lupus nephritis; circulating DNase inhibitors or anti-DNase antibodies in SLE impair DNase function and may drive autoimmunity flares.</cite> <cite id="33829021">Circulating NET levels are increased in SLE due to functional block of NET removal by anti-DNase antibodies or rare DNASE1L3 mutations; persistent NETs elevate free DNA/nucleosome components and oxidized proteins that can be recognized as non-self and presented to B cells via TLR9, driving IgG2 autoantibody formation; monitoring serum NETs may herald renal lesions and has clinical implications.</cite>

- Extracellular DNA and innate immune sensing fuel autoimmunity. Extracellular DNA from apoptotic and NETotic sources is endocytosed and induces type I interferon; this pathway is central to SLE pathogenesis, linking NET-derived DNA to interferon signaling and B-cell activation that produces pathogenic autoantibodies. <cite id="29553134">Extracellular DNA from apoptotic and NETotic cells stimulates innate immunity and induces type-I IFN after endocytosis, playing an important role in SLE pathogenesis.</cite>

- Anti-DNA immune complexes drive nephritis. In SLE, anti-DNA antibodies form immune complexes with circulating DNA (e.g., from NETs) that either deposit in kidneys to provoke lupus nephritis or are taken up by innate immune cells where they activate nucleic acid sensors, amplifying inflammatory signaling and autoantibody production. <cite id="38622070">Anti-DNA antibodies bind DNA to form immune complexes with two roles: renal deposition provoking nephritis and stimulation of cytokine production after uptake by innate immune cells via nucleic acid sensors; extracellular DNA can emerge from NETosis, providing immunologically active DNA that, together with ANAs, creates structures that promote systemic and organ inflammation and damage in SLE.</cite>

# Additional supporting observations

- SLE neutrophils are primed to release NETs, and this process can be induced by anti-DNA antibodies; persistent NETs are not efficiently cleared, favoring sustained antigen presentation and autoantibody generation. <cite id="38003689">Activated, interferon-primed SLE neutrophils are primed to release NETs on additional stimulation; anti-DNA antibodies may induce NET release and then bind NET DNA to protect it from digestion, increasing immunogenicity.</cite> <cite id="33829021">NET formation and removal are in balance in health; in SLE, blockage of removal by anti-DNase antibodies or DNASE1L3 mutations leads to persistent NETs and downstream autoimmunity, including TLR9-driven B-cell activation and IgG2 autoantibody formation, with prognostic value for renal lesions.</cite>

- Therapeutic implications reinforce causality. Targeting NET biology (e.g., PAD4 inhibitors, DNase supplementation) is proposed to reduce NET accumulation and autoimmunity in SLE and lupus nephritis, and clinical observations of anti-DNase autoantibodies and DNASE1L3 mutations linking to anti-dsDNA and nephritis support a mechanistic role. <cite id="27679792">Assessment of NET extent may inform IFN-α levels and identify SLE patients responsive to anti-IFN-α therapies or novel concepts such as N-acetyl-cysteine and PAD4 inhibitors that target NETs.</cite> <cite id="34685647">DNASE1/DNASE1L3 mutations cause anti-DNA formation and are associated with severe lupus-like syndromes and lupus nephritis; anti-DNase autoantibodies impair DNase function in SLE and may determine autoimmunity flares, suggesting that reducing NET accumulation could halt SLE and LN progression.</cite>

# Caveats and open questions

While the evidence strongly implicates NETs in SLE autoimmunity, some reviews note that autoantibodies against NET components are not the sole mechanism of tolerance breakdown, and other processes (e.g., hypercitrullination) may also contribute; moreover, simply inhibiting NETosis may be insufficient if latent infections persist. <cite id="27426444">Although autoantibodies to NET components are central, other mechanisms such as hypercitrullination can explain tolerance breakdown; continuous presentation of autoantigens mixed with intracellular pathogen antigens released by NETosis may be required to induce and sustain autoimmunity, and inhibiting NETosis alone may be insufficient if infections remain uncontrolled.</cite>

# Bottom line

Collectively, mechanistic studies, clinical correlations, and interventional hypotheses support that NETs are key drivers of loss of tolerance in SLE by exposing and stabilizing immunogenic dsDNA and nuclear antigens, activating interferon pathways, and serving as scaffolds for B-cell activation and antibody production; in practice, increased NETs associate with disease activity and lupus nephritis, and blocking NET accumulation or their clearance (via anti-DNase antibodies) correlates with anti-dsDNA formation and renal injury, reinforcing a causal role in autoantibody production and organ damage. <cite id="27679792,27426444,33746988,34685647,33829021,29553134,38003689,38622070">NETs expose cryptic autoepitopes and dsDNA antigens, correlate with SLE disease activity and renal disease, and their accumulation due to impaired clearance (anti-DNase autoantibodies or DNASE1L3 mutations) is linked to anti-dsDNA formation and lupus nephritis; anti-DNA antibodies can induce NET release and protect NET DNA from degradation, amplifying autoimmunity; extracellular DNA from NETs activates innate sensors and IFN pathways that drive autoantibody production and nephritis.</cite>

OBJECTIVES

# Summary of Consistently Reported Microbiome Alterations Linked to Glycemic Improvement After Bariatric Surgery

Across observational studies and preclinical models, several gut microbiome changes have been repeatedly associated with better glycemic control and remission of type 2 diabetes after bariatric surgery. However, findings vary by procedure and cohort, and mechanistic links are strongest when changes are tied to weight loss and inflammatory modulation.

- Akkermansia muciniphila expansion: Multiple studies report increased abundance of Akkermansia after bariatric procedures, including in diabetic animal models and human reviews, and associate this with improved fasting glucose and HbA1c. The bacterium is often framed as an "anti-inflammatory" mucin-degrading species whose rise may reflect improved mucosal health and barrier function that supports insulin sensitivity and glycemic control. <cite id="31197613">BS enables partial rescue of GM dysbiosis observed during obesity, with some characteristics modified post-BS linked to beneficial outcomes such as metabolic improvements</cite> <cite id="38863754">Single-anastomosis duodenal-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy increased Akkermansia in diabetic rats while decreasing fasting glucose and HbA1c</cite>.

- Bifidobacterium increase and Bacteroides decrease: Several reports, including in the SADI-S model, show higher Bifidobacterium (generally considered beneficial) and lower Bacteroides (often associated with pro-inflammatory or pro-diabetic profiles), coinciding with improved glycemia. These compositional shifts are linked to lower alpha-diversity and a shift toward anti-inflammatory taxa that may favor glucose homeostasis. <cite id="38863754">SADI-S significantly increased anti-inflammatory bacteria (Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium) and decreased pro-inflammatory bacteria (Bacteroides), alongside reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c</cite> <cite id="31197613">Post-surgical GM changes in composition and function are linked to weight loss and metabolic improvements, though variability is high</cite>.

- Shifts in mucin-degrading and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing taxa: Reviews emphasize that bariatric surgery partially reverses obesity-associated dysbiosis, including taxa involved in mucin degradation and fermentation that influence inflammation and insulin signaling. These shifts often accompany improved HbA1c and fasting glucose, though the precise causal pathways remain under study. <cite id="31197613">BS-induced partial rescue of dysbiosis includes compositional and functional alterations that correlate with clinical metabolic improvements</cite>.

- Decreased alpha-diversity and pro-inflammatory profiles: Across procedures, reduced Shannon diversity and lower richness are frequently observed alongside increases in anti-inflammatory taxa, which may reflect improved endotoxemia and systemic inflammation—factors known to impair insulin action. These changes tend to coincide with better glycemic outcomes. <cite id="38863754">Compared with sham-operated controls, SADI-S reduced species richness and increased evenness (lower Shannon, higher Simpson), with associated glycemic improvements</cite> <cite id="31197613">Changes in GM post-BS display variability, but features linked to metabolic improvements are reproducible at an aggregate level</cite>.

- Correlative links to HbA1c and glucose: In animal models, specific taxa show inverse correlations with glycemic markers; higher Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundances correlate with lower fasting glucose and HbA1c, whereas higher Bacteroides associates with worse control. These correlations support a role for microbiome remodeling in glycemic remission, particularly when aligned with caloric restriction and gut hormonal changes after surgery. <cite id="38863754">Blood glucose correlated positively with Bacteroides and negatively with Bifidobacterium; SADI-S lowered both fasting glucose and HbA1c alongside microbiome shifts</cite>.

# Interpretation and Caveats

- Consistency vs. heterogeneity: Increases in Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium and decreases in Bacteroides, along with reduced alpha-diversity and mucin-degrading/SCFA-axis shifts, recur across studies and models as correlates of improved glycemia. Yet inter-patient variability is substantial, and not all surgical procedures yield identical microbiome trajectories, limiting universal predictors of remission. <cite id="31197613">Post-BS GM changes vary widely between individuals, though certain features align with improved metabolic outcomes</cite>.

- Causality and mechanisms: While associations are strong, causal pathways likely involve multiple interacting axes—microbial composition, mucosal barrier function, endotoxemia, and postsurgical hormonal signals (e.g., incretins). Translational studies and longitudinal human cohorts are needed to disentangle which changes drive glycemic improvement versus result from weight loss and inflammation reduction. <cite id="31197613">Further large-sample studies and microbial transfer models are required to fully define the role of GM in post-surgical clinical improvements</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways for Glycemic Control

- Expect microbiome features that point to reduced inflammation and improved mucosal integrity (e.g., Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium increases; Bacteroides decreases) to accompany remission in many responders, particularly after procedures that combine restriction and malabsorption (e.g., duodenal switch/ileal-y, SADI-S). <cite id="38863754">SADI-S produced anti-inflammatory taxa increases and pro-inflammatory taxa decreases with improved glycemic markers</cite>.

- Track alpha-diversity and richness shifts alongside functional pathways (mucin degradation, fermentation) as potential biomarkers of response, recognizing high inter-individual variability and the need for longitudinal integration with glycemic endpoints. <cite id="31197613">Post-BS GM compositional and functional changes correlate with metabolic improvements but exhibit notable variability</cite>.
</answer>

These shifts often accompany improved HbA1c and fasting glucose, though the precise causal pathways remain under study. <cite id="31197613">BS-induced partial rescue of dysbiosis includes compositional and functional alterations that correlate with clinical metabolic improvements</cite>.

- Decreased alpha-diversity and pro-inflammatory profiles: Across procedures, reduced Shannon diversity and lower richness are frequently observed alongside increases in anti-inflammatory taxa, which may reflect improved endotoxemia and systemic inflammation—factors known to impair insulin action. These changes tend to coincide with better glycemic outcomes. <cite id="38863754">Compared with sham-operated controls, SADI-S reduced species richness and increased evenness (lower Shannon, higher Simpson), with associated glycemic improvements</cite> <cite id="31197613">Changes in GM post-BS display variability, but features linked to metabolic improvements are reproducible at an aggregate level</cite>.

- Correlative links to HbA1c and glucose: In animal models, specific taxa show inverse correlations with glycemic markers; higher Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia abundances correlate with lower fasting glucose and HbA1c, whereas higher Bacteroides associates with worse control. These correlations support a role for microbiome remodeling in glycemic remission, particularly when aligned with caloric restriction and gut hormonal changes after surgery. <cite id="38863754">Blood glucose correlated positively with Bacteroides and negatively with Bifidobacterium; SADI-S lowered both fasting glucose and HbA1c alongside microbiome shifts</cite>.

# Interpretation and Caveats

- Consistency vs. heterogeneity: Increases in Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium and decreases in Bacteroides, along with reduced alpha-diversity and mucin-degrading/SCFA-axis shifts, recur across studies and models as correlates of improved glycemia. Yet inter-patient variability is substantial, and not all surgical procedures yield identical microbiome trajectories, limiting universal predictors of remission. <cite id="31197613">Post-BS GM changes vary widely between individuals, though certain features align with improved metabolic outcomes</cite>.

- Causality and mechanisms: While associations are strong, causal pathways likely involve multiple interacting axes—microbial composition, mucosal barrier function, endotoxemia, and postsurgical hormonal signals (e.g., incretins). Translational studies and longitudinal human cohorts are needed to disentangle which changes drive glycemic improvement versus result from weight loss and inflammation reduction. <cite id="31197613">Further large-sample studies and microbial transfer models are required to fully define the role of GM in post-surgical clinical improvements</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways for Glycemic Control

- Expect microbiome features that point to reduced inflammation and improved mucosal integrity (e.g., Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium increases; Bacteroides decreases) to accompany remission in many responders, particularly after procedures that combine restriction and malabsorption (e.g., duodenal switch/ileal-y, SADI-S). <cite id="38863754">SADI-S produced anti-inflammatory taxa increases and pro-inflammatory taxa decreases with improved glycemic markers</cite>.

- Track alpha-diversity and richness shifts alongside functional pathways (mucin degradation, fermentation) as potential biomarkers of response, recognizing high inter-individual variability and the need for longitudinal integration with glycemic endpoints. <cite id="31197613">Post-BS GM compositional and functional changes correlate with metabolic improvements but exhibit notable variability</cite>.

<snippet id="34551229">Title: Overall Survival Benefit with Tebentafusp in Metastatic Uveal Melanoma.
Authors: Nathan, Paul, Hassel, Jessica C, Rutkowski, Piotr et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Uveal melanoma is a disease that is distinct from cutaneous melanoma, with a low tumor mutational burden and a 1-year overall survival of approximately 50% in patients with metastatic uveal melanoma. Data showing a proven overall survival benefit with a systemic treatment are lacking. Tebentafusp is a bispecific protein consisting of an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor fused to an anti-CD3 effector that can redirect T cells to target glycoprotein 100-positive cells.
METHODS
In this open-label, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned previously untreated HLA-A*02:01-positive patients with metastatic uveal melanoma in a 2:1 ratio to receive tebentafusp (tebentafusp group) or the investigator's choice of therapy with single-agent pembrolizumab, ipilimumab, or dacarbazine (control group), stratified according to the lactate dehydrogenase level. The primary end point was overall survival.
RESULTS
A total of 378 patients were randomly assigned to either the tebentafusp group (252 patients) or the control group (126 patients). Overall survival at 1 year was 73% in the tebentafusp group and 59% in the control group (hazard ratio for death, 0.51; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.37 to 0.71; P<0.001) in the intention-to-treat population. Progression-free survival was also significantly higher in the tebentafusp group than in the control group (31% vs. 19% at 6 months; hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.58 to 0.94; P = 0.01). The most common treatment-related adverse events in the tebentafusp group were cytokine-mediated events (due to T-cell activation) and skin-related events (due to glycoprotein 100-positive melanocytes), including rash (83%), pyrexia (76%), and pruritus (69%). These adverse events decreased in incidence and severity after the first three or four doses and infrequently led to discontinuation of the trial treatment (2%). No treatment-related deaths were reported.
CONCLUSIONS
Treatment with tebentafusp resulted in longer overall survival than the control therapy among previously untreated patients with metastatic uveal melanoma. (Funded by Immunocore; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03070392; EudraCT number, 2015-003153-18.).</snippet>
<snippet id="39062758">Title: Immunotherapy in Breast Cancer.
Authors: Dvir, Kathrin, Giordano, Sara, Leone, Jose Pablo | Year: 2024 | Journal: International journal of molecular sciences
Abstract: Breast cancer is a disease encompassing a spectrum of molecular subtypes and clinical presentations, each with distinct prognostic implications and treatment responses. Breast cancer has traditionally been considered an immunologically "cold" tumor, unresponsive to immunotherapy. However, clinical trials in recent years have found immunotherapy to be an efficacious therapeutic option for select patients. Breast cancer is categorized into different subtypes ranging from the most common positive hormone receptor (HR+), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative type, to less frequent HER2- positive breast cancer and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), highlighting the necessity for tailored treatment strategies aimed at maximizing patient outcomes. Despite notable progress in early detection and new therapeutic modalities, breast cancer remains the second leading cause of cancer death in the USA. Moreover, in recent decades, breast cancer incidence rates have been increasing, especially in women younger than the age of 50. This has prompted the exploration of new therapeutic approaches to address this trend, offering new therapeutic prospects for breast cancer patients. Immunotherapy is a class of therapeutic agents that has revolutionized the treatment landscape of many cancers, namely melanoma, lung cancer, and gastroesophageal cancers, amongst others. Though belatedly, immunotherapy has entered the treatment armamentarium of breast cancer, with the approval of pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) in the neoadjuvant and advanced settings, thereby paving the path for further research and integration of immune checkpoint inhibitors in other subtypes of breast cancer. Trials exploring various combination therapies to harness the power of immunotherapy in symbiosis with various chemotherapeutic agents are ongoing in hopes of improving response rates and prolonging survival for breast cancer patients. Biomarkers and precise patient selection for the utilization of immunotherapy remain cardinal and are currently under investigation, with some biomarkers showing promise, such as Program Death Lignat-1 (PDL-1) Combined Positive Score, Tumor Mutation Burden (TMB), and Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TILs). This review will present the current landscape of immunotherapy, particularly checkpoint inhibitors, in different types of breast cancer.</snippet>
<snippet id="34999237">Title: Metastatic uveal melanoma: The final frontier.
Authors: Rantala, Elina S, Hernberg, Micaela M, Piperno-Neumann, Sophie et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Progress in retinal and eye research
Abstract: Treatment of primary intraocular uveal melanoma has developed considerably, its driver genes are largely unraveled, and the ways to assess its risk for metastases are very precise, being based on an international staging system and genetic data. Unfortunately, the risk of distant metastases, which emerge in approximately one half of all patients, is unaltered. Metastases are the leading single cause of death after uveal melanoma is diagnosed, yet no consensus exists regarding surveillance, staging, and treatment of disseminated disease, and survival has not improved until recently. The final frontier in conquering uveal melanoma lies in solving these issues to cure metastatic disease. Most studies on metastatic uveal melanoma are small, uncontrolled, retrospective, and do not report staging. Meta-analyses confirm a median overall survival of 10-13 months, and a cure rate that approaches nil, although survival exceeding 5 years is possible, estimated 2% either with first-line treatment or with best supportive care. Hepatic ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging as surveillance methods have a sensitivity of 95-100% and 83-100%, respectively, to detect metastases without radiation hazard according to prevailing evidence, but computed tomography is necessary for staging. No blood-based tests additional to liver function tests are generally accepted. Three validated staging systems predict, each in defined situations, overall survival after metastasis. Their essential components include measures of tumor burden, liver function, and performance status or metastasis free interval. Age and gender may additionally influence survival. Exceptional mutational events in metastases may make them susceptible to checkpoint inhibitors. In a large meta-analysis, surgical treatment was associated with 6 months longer median overall survival as compared to conventional chemotherapy and, recently, tebentafusp as first-line treatment at the first interim analysis of a randomized phase III trial likewise provided a 6 months longer median overall survival compared to investigator's choice, mostly pembrolizumab; these treatments currently apply to selected patients. Promoting dormancy of micrometastases, harmonizing surveillance protocols, promoting staging, identifying predictive factors, initiating controlled clinical trials, and standardizing reporting will be critical steppingstones in reaching the final frontier of curing metastatic uveal melanoma.</snippet>
<snippet id="40847234">Title: Immunotherapy in Melanoma.
Authors: Xing, Yan, Wu, Helena T, Rajurkar, Swapnil et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Cancer treatment and research
Abstract: This chapter explores systemic treatment strategies for cutaneous melanoma across neoadjuvant, adjuvant, and Stage IV settings. Neoadjuvant therapy aims to reduce tumor burden pre-surgery, primarily using immune checkpoint inhibitors like nivolumab plus ipilimumab, showing promising response rates. Adjuvant therapy, post-resection, leverages immunotherapy (e.g., nivolumab) and targeted therapies (e.g., dabrafenib plus trametinib) to prevent recurrence in high-risk patients, improving relapse-free survival. Stage IV systemic treatment addresses metastatic disease, employing immunotherapy (nivolumab, pembrolizumab) and targeted mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway inhibitors (dabrafenib plus trametinib) for BRAF-mutant cases, while BRAF wild-type patients benefit from nivolumab-relatlimab or combination therapies. Tables summarize key regimens, efficacy, and toxicities. Content aligns with clinical guidelines, with updates on emerging therapies like tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL). These approaches enhance survival and treatment-free intervals, tailored to mutation status and disease stage.</snippet>
<snippet id="36358851">Title: Interplay between Tumor Mutational Burden and Mutational Profile and Its Effect on Overall Survival: A Pilot Study of Metastatic Patients Treated with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors.
Authors: Xavier, Camila B, Lopes, Carlos Diego H, Awni, Beatriz M et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Cancers
Abstract: Purpose: Solid tumors harboring tumor mutational burden (TMB) ≥10 mutations per megabase (mut/Mb) received agnostic approval for pembrolizumab. This work aims to analyze the somatic mutational profile’s influence on the outcomes of patients with TMB-high tumors treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Methods: This post-hoc analysis evaluated clinical and molecular features of patients with solid tumors treated with ICIs that could be either monoclonal antibody directed against programmed cell death protein-1 or monoclonal antibody directed against programmed cell death ligand 1 (anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1), monoclonal antibody directed against cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen (anti-CTLA-4) or a combined treatment regimen including one anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 and one anti-CTLA-4 (ICIs combination). We performed OS analysis for TMB thresholds of ≥10, ≥20, and <10 mut/Mb. We assessed OS according to the mutational profile for a TMB ≥ 10 mut/Mb cutoff. For genes correlated with OS at the univariate assessment, we conducted a Cox multivariate analysis adjusted by median TMB, sex, age, microsatellite instability (MSI), and histology. Results: A total of 1661 patients were investigated; 488 with a TMB ≥10 mut/Mb (29.4%). The median OS was 42 months for TMB ≥10 or 20 mut/Mb, and 15 months for TMB <10 mut/Mb (p < 0.005). Among TMB ≥10 mut/Mb patients, mutations in E2F3 or STK11 correlated with worse OS, and mutations in NTRK3, PTPRD, RNF43, TENT5C, TET1, or ZFHX3 with better OS. These associations were confirmed with univariate and multivariate analyses (p < 0.05). Melanoma histology and TMB above the median endowed patients with better OS (p < 0.05), while MSI status, age, and gender did not have a statistically significant effect on OS. Conclusion: Combining TMB and mutation profiles in key cancer genes can better qualify patients for ICI treatment and predict their OS.</snippet>

<snippet id="32738738">Title: Impact of high tumor mutational burden in solid tumors and challenges for biomarker application.
Authors: McNamara, Mairéad G, Jacobs, Timothy, Lamarca, Angela et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Cancer treatment reviews
Abstract: Accurate identification of patients with solid tumors likely to respond to immunotherapy is crucial. Tumor mutational burden (TMB) measures the number of somatic mutations in a tumor and is an emerging prognostic and predictive biomarker for anti-programmed cell death (PD) 1/anti-PD-ligand 1 therapy and other immunotherapeutic agents. Tumor mutational burden is assessed optimally by whole exome sequencing, but next generation sequencing provides TMB estimates in a more timely and cost-effective manner. Blood-based measurement of TMB in plasma offers an alternative to the need for adequate tumor tissue for molecular testing, and has demonstrated the ability to identify patients who derive benefit from immunotherapy. Tumor mutational burden has diverse prognostic impact in different solid tumor types and also has a demonstrated role in predicting improved survival in patients receiving immunotherapy. There are challenges to TMB adoption into standard clinical practice, including variations in its definition, with the mutational number defining TMB-high appearing to vary across cancer types. The magnitude of TMB also varies across different tumor types, with the highest levels reported in melanoma and other skin cancers (where ultraviolet light is the dominant mutational process), followed by non-small cell lung cancer and other squamous carcinomas. Concerns regarding inter-laboratory and inter-platform variations in analysis methods have been raised, highlighting the need for standardization. Integration of other genomic or pathological biomarkers with TMB may increase its prognostic and predictive capabilities and validation of individual or combination models in prospective trials is warranted.</snippet>
<snippet id="38848517">Title: Predictive Impact of Tumor Mutational Burden on Real-World Outcomes of First-Line Immune Checkpoint Inhibition in Metastatic Melanoma.
Authors: Andrews, Miles C, Li, Gerald, Graf, Ryon P et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: JCO precision oncology
Abstract: PURPOSE
The choice of threshold and reliability of high tumor mutational burden (TMB) to predict outcomes and guide treatment choice for patients with metastatic melanoma receiving first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in the real world is not well known.
METHODS
Using a deidentified nationwide (US-based) melanoma clinicogenomic database, we identified a real-world cohort of patients with metastatic melanoma (N = 497) who received first-line monotherapy anti-PD-1 (n = 240) or dual anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 ICI (n = 257) and had a tissue-based comprehensive genomic profiling test TMB score.
RESULTS
TMB-high (TMB-H; ≥10 mutations per megabase [muts/Mb], n = 352, 71%) was independently predictive of superior real-world progression-free survival and overall survival versus TMB-low (<10 mut/Mb, n = 145, 29%) in both mono ICI (hazard ratio [HR], 0.45 [95% CI, 0.32 to 0.63]; P < .001; HR, 0.61 [95% CI, 0.41 to 0.90]; P = .01, respectively) and dual ICI (HR, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.49 to 0.90]; P = .009; HR, 0.61 [95% CI, 0.42 to 0.88]; P = .007, respectively) patients. Dual ICI offered no significant advantage in BRAF wt patients and unexpectedly demonstrated greatest benefit in the TMB 10-19 mut/Mb group, identifying a TMB-very high (≥20 mut/Mb, n = 247, 50%) BRAF mut patient subgroup for whom mono ICI may be preferable.
CONCLUSION
TMB-H predicts superior outcomes on ICI while coassessment of BRAF status and TMB may inform first-line regimen choice.</snippet>
<snippet id="40874224">Title: Adjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy improves melanoma-specific survival in stage IIIC-IV melanoma patients with high tumor mutation burden and BRAF V600 mutation.
Authors: Forschner, Julia, Huynh, Julia, Schroeder, Christopher et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Frontiers in oncology
Abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) have significantly improved melanoma-specific survival (MSS), particularly in patients with tumors with a high tumor mutational burden (TMB) or BRAF mutation. In the adjuvant setting, ICIs significantly improve relapse-free survival (RFS), but data on MSS are still lacking. Tissue samples from 83 patients with stage IIIC/D/IV melanoma who started adjuvant ICI between March 2018 and September 2019 were examined using a 700 gene panel. TMB and BRAF V600E/K mutation status were analyzed to determine their potential influence on RFS and MSS. TMB levels ≥ 20 Var/Mb were classified as TMB high, corresponding to the top 20% TMB levels in the cohort. RFS and MSS were significantly improved in patients whose tumors had high TMB levels and BRAF V600E/K mutation (p<0.001 and p=0.002, respectively). Patients with BRAF -mutated tumors and high TMB seem to benefit particularly from adjuvant ICI.</snippet>
<snippet id="31300034">Title: Tumor mutation burden and circulating tumor DNA in combined CTLA-4 and PD-1 antibody therapy in metastatic melanoma - results of a prospective biomarker study.
Authors: Forschner, Andrea, Battke, Florian, Hadaschik, Dirk et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Journal for immunotherapy of cancer
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Metastasized or unresectable melanoma has been the first malignant tumor to be successfully treated with checkpoint inhibitors. Nevertheless, about 40-50% of the patients do not respond to these treatments and severe side effects are observed in up to 60%. Therefore, there is a high need to identify reliable biomarkers predicting response. Tumor Mutation Burden (TMB) is a debated predictor for response to checkpoint inhibitors and early measurement of ctDNA can help to detect treatment failure to immunotherapy in selected melanoma patients. However, it has not yet been clarified how TMB and ctDNA can be used to estimate response to combined CTLA-4 and PD-1 antibody therapy in metastatic melanoma.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
In this prospective biomarker study, we included 35 melanoma patients with ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) and nivolumab (anti-PD-1) therapy. In all patients, a tumor panel of 710 tumor-associated genes was applied (tumor vs. reference tissue comparison), followed by repetitive liquid biopsies. Cell-free DNA was extracted and at least one driver mutation was monitored. Treatment response was evaluated after about three months of therapy.
RESULTS
TMB was significantly higher in responders than in nonresponders and TMB > 23.1 Mut/Mb (TMB-high) was associated with a survival benefit compared to TMB ≤ 23.1 Mut/Mb (TMB-low or TMB-intermediate). Furthermore, a > 50% decrease of cell-free DNA concentration or undetectable circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), measured by tumor-specific variant copies/ml of plasma at first follow-up three weeks after treatment initiation were significantly associated with response to combined immunotherapy and improved overall survival, respectively. It is noticeable that no patient with TMB ≤ 23.1 Mut/Mb and detectable or increasing ctDNA at first follow-up responded to immunotherapy.
CONCLUSION
High TMB, > 50% decrease of cell-free DNA concentration, and undetectable ctDNA at first follow-up seem to be associated with response and overall survival under combined immunotherapy. The evaluation of ctDNA and cell-free DNA three weeks after treatment initiation may be suitable for early assessment of efficacy of immunotherapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="38341515">Title: ARID2 mutations may relay a distinct subset of cutaneous melanoma patients with different outcomes.
Authors: Akinjiyan, Favour A, Nassief, George, Phillipps, Jordan et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Scientific reports
Abstract: ARID genes encode subunits of SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes and are frequently mutated in human cancers. We investigated the correlation between ARID mutations, molecular features, and clinical outcomes in melanoma patients. Cutaneous melanoma samples (n = 1577) were analyzed by next-generation sequencing. Samples were stratified by pathogenic/likely pathogenic mutation in ARID genes (ARID1A/2/1B/5B). PD-L1 expression was assessed using IHC (SP142; positive (+): ≥ 1%). Tumor mutation burden (TMB)-high was defined as ≥ 10 mutations/Mb. Transcriptomic signatures predictive of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors-interferon gamma and T-cell inflamed score were calculated. Real-world overall survival (OS) information was obtained from insurance claims data, with Kaplan-Meier estimates calculated from time of tissue collection until last date of contact. Mann-Whitney U, Chi-square, and Fisher exact tests were applied where appropriate, with p values adjusted for multiple comparisons. ARID2 mutations were more prevalent in cutaneous melanoma compared to ARID1A (11.0%: n = 451 vs 2.8%: n = 113), with concurrent ARID1A/ARID2 mutation in 1.1% (n = 46) of samples. ARID mutations were associated with a high prevalence of RAS pathway mutations-NF1 (ARID1A, 52.6%; ARID2, 48.5%; ARID1A/2, 63.6%; and ARID-WT, 13.3%; p < 0.0001) and KRAS (ARID1A, 3.5%; ARID2, 3.1%; ARID1A/2, 6.5%; and ARID-WT, 1.0%; p = 0.018)), although BRAF mutations were less common in ARID-mutated cohorts (ARID1A, 31.9%; ARID2, 35.6%; ARID1A/2, 26.1%; and ARID-WT, 50.4%; p < 0.0001). TMB-high was more common in ARID-mutated samples (ARID1A, 80.9%; ARID2, 89.9%; ARID1A/2, 100%; and ARID-WT, 49.4%; p < 0.0001), while PD-L1 positivity was similar across subgroups (ARID1A, 43.8%; ARID2, 51.1%; ARID1A/2, 52.5%; and ARID-WT, 44.9%; p = 0.109). Patients with ARID1A mutations had a higher prevalence of dMMR/MSI-H compared to those with ARID-WT (2.7% vs 0.2%, p = 0.030). Median IFN-γ and T-cell signatures were higher in ARID2-mutated samples compared to ARID-WT (IFN-γ: - 0.15 vs - 0.21, p = 0.0066; T-cell: 23.5 vs - 18.5, p = 0.041). ARID2-mutated patients had improved survival compared to ARID-WT; (HR: 1.22 (95% CI 1.0-1.5), p = 0.022). No additional OS benefit was observed with anti-PD-1 therapy for ARID2 mutation compared to ARID-WT. Melanoma patients with ARID mutations exhibited higher prevalence of markers associated with ICI response, including TMB-H, and immune-related signatures. Our data also suggests improved survival outcome in patients with ARID2 mutations, irrespective of anti-PD1 therapy.</snippet>

<snippet id="30505709">Title: Clinical utility of tumor mutational burden in patients with non-small cell lung cancer treated with immunotherapy.
Authors: Hendriks, Lizza E, Rouleau, Etienne, Besse, Benjamin | Year: 2018 | Journal: Translational lung cancer research
Abstract: Anti-programmed death (ligand)-1 [anti-PD-(L)1] therapies such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab or atezolizumab have become standard of care for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients either in first line or beyond. PD-L1 expression level allows enriching the treated population with responders, but it is still not an optimal biomarker. Even in patients with PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) levels of ≥50% treated with first line pembrolizumab overall response rate (ORR) is only 44.8% and overall survival at one year is 70%. Moreover, in combination trials with chemotherapy and anti-PD-(L)1 therapy, a significant proportion of patients does not respond (ORR ranges from 45.3% to 64.0%), regardless of PD-L1 expression. Furthermore, PD-L1 expression level is not associated with improved benefit in patients treated with combinations of anti-PD-(L)1 and anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen (anti-CTLA4) therapy. One of the new promising biomarkers is tumor mutational burden (TMB). It has been discovered that especially tumor types with a known high mutation rate such as NSCLC and melanoma respond best to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). An explanation is that this high mutation rate makes it more likely that neoantigens arise that are targeted by activated immune cells, but it is not feasible to determine neoantigen load in daily practice. However, TMB of a certain tumor type is associated with neoantigen load and outcome on ICIs. In this comprehensive review, we discuss the TMB analysis methods, the rationale to use TMB as a predictive biomarker and the clinical utility of TMB in NSCLC patients treated with ICIs.</snippet>
<snippet id="30002656">Title: Biomarkers for Clinical Benefit of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Treatment-A Review From the Melanoma Perspective and Beyond.
Authors: Buder-Bakhaya, Kristina, Hassel, Jessica C | Year: 2018 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) with anti-CTLA-4 and/or anti-PD-1 antibodies is standard treatment for metastatic melanoma. Anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) and anti-PD-L1 antibodies (atezolizumab, durvalumab, and avelumab) have been approved for treatment of several other advanced malignancies, including non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC); renal cell, and urothelial carcinoma; head and neck cancer; gastric, hepatocellular, and Merkel-cell carcinoma; and classical Hodgkin lymphoma. In some of these malignancies approval was based on the detection of biomarkers such as PD-L1 expression or high microsatellite instability.
METHODS
We review the current status of prognostic and predictive biomarkers used in ICI for melanoma and other malignancies. We include clinical, tissue, blood, and stool biomarkers, as well as imaging biomarkers.
RESULTS
Several biomarkers have been studied in ICI for metastatic melanoma. In clinical practice, pre-treatment tumor burden measured by means of imaging and serum lactate dehydrogenase level is already being used to estimate the likelihood of effective ICI treatment. In peripheral blood, the number of different immune cell types, such as lymphocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils, as well as different soluble factors, have been correlated with clinical outcome. For intra-tumoral biomarkers, expression of the PD-1 ligand PD-L1 has been found to be of some predictive value for anti-PD-1-directed therapy for NSCLC and melanoma. A high mutational load, particularly when accompanied by neoantigens, seems to facilitate immune response and correlates with patient survival for all entities treated by use of ICI. Tumor microenvironment also seems to be of major importance. Interestingly, even the gut microbiome has been found to correlate with response to ICI, most likely through immuno-stimulatory effects of distinct bacteria. New imaging biomarkers, e.g., for PET, and magnetic resonance imaging are also being investigated, and results suggest they will make early prediction of patient response possible.
CONCLUSION
Several promising results are available regarding possible biomarkers for response to ICI, which need to be validated in large clinical trials. A better understanding of how ICI works will enable the development of biomarkers that can predict the response of individual patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="34785583">Title: A PD-1/PD-L1 Proximity Assay as a Theranostic Marker for PD-1 Blockade in Patients with Metastatic Melanoma.
Authors: Girault, Isabelle, Adam, Julien, Shen, Shensi et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research
Abstract: PURPOSE
Less than 50% of patients with melanoma respond to anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1), and this treatment can induce severe toxicity. Predictive markers are thus needed to improve the benefit/risk ratio of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). Baseline tumor parameters such as programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, CD8 + T-cell infiltration, mutational burden, and various transcriptomic signatures are associated with response to ICI, but their predictive values are not sufficient. Interaction between PD-1 and its main ligand, PD-L1, appears as a valuable target of anti-PD-1 therapy. Thus, instead of looking at PD-L1 expression only, we evaluated the predictive value of the proximity between PD-1 and its neighboring PD-L1 molecules in terms of response to anti-PD-1 therapy.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
PD-1/PD-L1 proximity was assessed by proximity ligation assay (PLA) on 137 samples from two cohorts (exploratory n = 66 and validation n = 71) of samples from patients with melanoma treated with anti-PD-1±anti-CTLA-4. Additional predictive biomarkers, such as PD-L1 expression (MELscore), CD8 + cells density, and NanoString RNA signature, were also evaluated.
RESULTS
A PD-1/PD-L1 PLA model was developed to predict tumor response in an exploratory cohort and further evaluated in an independent validation cohort. This score showed higher predictive ability (AUC = 0.85 and 0.79 in the two cohorts, respectively) for PD-1/PD-L1 PLA as compared with other parameters (AUC = 0.71-0.77). Progression-free and overall survival were significantly longer in patients with high PLA values ( P = 0.00019 and P < 0.0001, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS
The proximity between PD-1 and PD-L1, easily assessed by this PLA on one formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded section, appears as a new biomarker of anti-PD-1 efficacy.</snippet>

data.title: Overall Survival Benefit with Tebentafusp in Metastatic Uveal Melanoma.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Uveal melanoma is a disease that is distinct from cutaneous melanoma, with a low tumor mutational burden and a 1-year overall survival of approximately 50% in patients with metastatic uveal melanoma. Data showing a proven overall survival benefit with a systemic treatment are lacking. Tebentafusp is a bispecific protein consisting of an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor fused to an anti-CD3 effector that can redirect T cells to target glycoprotein 100-positive cells.
METHODS
In this open-label, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned previously untreated HLA-A*02:01-positive patients with metastatic uveal melanoma in a 2:1 ratio to receive tebentafusp (tebentafusp group) or the investigator's choice of therapy with single-agent pembrolizumab, ipilimumab, or dacarbazine (control group), stratified according to the lactate dehydrogenase level. The primary end point was overall survival.
RESULTS
A total of 378 patients were randomly assigned to either the tebentafusp group (252 patients) or the control group (126 patients). Overall survival at 1 year was 73% in the tebentafusp group and 59% in the control group (hazard ratio for death, 0.51; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.37 to 0.71; P<0.001) in the intention-to-treat population. Progression-free survival was also significantly higher in the tebentafusp group than in the control group (31% vs. 19% at 6 months; hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.58 to 0.94; P = 0.01). The most common treatment-related adverse events in the tebentafusp group were cytokine-mediated events (due to T-cell activation) and skin-related events (due to glycoprotein 100-positive melanocytes), including rash (83%), pyrexia (76%), and pruritus (69%). These adverse events decreased in incidence and severity after the first three or four doses and infrequently led to discontinuation of the trial treatment (2%). No treatment-related deaths were reported.
CONCLUSIONS
Treatment with tebentafusp resulted in longer overall survival than the control therapy among previously untreated patients with metastatic uveal melanoma. (Funded by Immunocore; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03070392; EudraCT number, 2015-003153-18.).

data.title: Immunotherapy in Breast Cancer.
data.abstract: Breast cancer is a disease encompassing a spectrum of molecular subtypes and clinical presentations, each with distinct prognostic implications and treatment responses. Breast cancer has traditionally been considered an immunologically "cold" tumor, unresponsive to immunotherapy. However, clinical trials in recent years have found immunotherapy to be an efficacious therapeutic option for select patients. Breast cancer is categorized into different subtypes ranging from the most common positive hormone receptor (HR+), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative type, to less frequent HER2- positive breast cancer and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), highlighting the necessity for tailored treatment strategies aimed at maximizing patient outcomes. Despite notable progress in early detection and new therapeutic modalities, breast cancer remains the second leading cause of cancer death in the USA. Moreover, in recent decades, breast cancer incidence rates have been increasing, especially in women younger than the age of 50. This has prompted the exploration of new therapeutic approaches to address this trend, offering new therapeutic prospects for breast cancer patients. Immunotherapy is a class of therapeutic agents that has revolutionized the treatment landscape of many cancers, namely melanoma, lung cancer, and gastroesophageal cancers, amongst others. Though belatedly, immunotherapy has entered the treatment armamentarium of breast cancer, with the approval of pembrolizumab in combination with chemotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) in the neoadjuvant and advanced settings, thereby paving the path for further research and integration of immune checkpoint inhibitors in other subtypes of breast cancer. Trials exploring various combination therapies to harness the power of immunotherapy in symbiosis with various chemotherapeutic agents are ongoing in hopes of improving response rates and prolonging survival for breast cancer patients. Biomarkers and precise patient selection for the utilization of immunotherapy remain cardinal and are currently under investigation, with some biomarkers showing promise, such as Program Death Lignat-1 (PDL-1) Combined Positive Score, Tumor Mutation Burden (TMB), and Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TILs). This review will present the current landscape of immunotherapy, particularly checkpoint inhibitors, in different types of breast cancer.

data.title: Metastatic uveal melanoma: The final frontier.
data.abstract: Treatment of primary intraocular uveal melanoma has developed considerably, its driver genes are largely unraveled, and the ways to assess its risk for metastases are very precise, being based on an international staging system and genetic data. Unfortunately, the risk of distant metastases, which emerge in approximately one half of all patients, is unaltered. Metastases are the leading single cause of death after uveal melanoma is diagnosed, yet no consensus exists regarding surveillance, staging, and treatment of disseminated disease, and survival has not improved until recently. The final frontier in conquering uveal melanoma lies in solving these issues to cure metastatic disease. Most studies on metastatic uveal melanoma are small, uncontrolled, retrospective, and do not report staging. Meta-analyses confirm a median overall survival of 10-13 months, and a cure rate that approaches nil, although survival exceeding 5 years is possible, estimated 2% either with first-line treatment or with best supportive care. Hepatic ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging as surveillance methods have a sensitivity of 95-100% and 83-100%, respectively, to detect metastases without radiation hazard according to prevailing evidence, but computed tomography is necessary for staging. No blood-based tests additional to liver function tests are generally accepted. Three validated staging systems predict, each in defined situations, overall survival after metastasis. Their essential components include measures of tumor burden, liver function, and performance status or metastasis free interval. Age and gender may additionally influence survival. Exceptional mutational events in metastases may make them susceptible to checkpoint inhibitors. In a large meta-analysis, surgical treatment was associated with 6 months longer median overall survival as compared to conventional chemotherapy and, recently, tebentafusp as first-line treatment at the first interim analysis of a randomized phase III trial likewise provided a 6 months longer median overall survival compared to investigator's choice, mostly pembrolizumab; these treatments currently apply to selected patients. Promoting dormancy of micrometastases, harmonizing surveillance protocols, promoting staging, identifying predictive factors, initiating controlled clinical trials, and standardizing reporting will be critical steppingstones in reaching the final frontier of curing metastatic uveal melanoma.

data.title: Immunotherapy in Melanoma.
data.abstract: This chapter explores systemic treatment strategies for cutaneous melanoma across neoadjuvant, adjuvant, and Stage IV settings. Neoadjuvant therapy aims to reduce tumor burden pre-surgery, primarily using immune checkpoint inhibitors like nivolumab plus ipilimumab, showing promising response rates. Adjuvant therapy, post-resection, leverages immunotherapy (e.g., nivolumab) and targeted therapies (e.g., dabrafenib plus trametinib) to prevent recurrence in high-risk patients, improving relapse-free survival. Stage IV systemic treatment addresses metastatic disease, employing immunotherapy (nivolumab, pembrolizumab) and targeted mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway inhibitors (dabrafenib plus trametinib) for BRAF-mutant cases, while BRAF wild-type patients benefit from nivolumab-relatlimab or combination therapies. Tables summarize key regimens, efficacy, and toxicities. Content aligns with clinical guidelines, with updates on emerging therapies like tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL). These approaches enhance survival and treatment-free intervals, tailored to mutation status and disease stage.

data.title: Interplay between Tumor Mutational Burden and Mutational Profile and Its Effect on Overall Survival: A Pilot Study of Metastatic Patients Treated with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors.
data.abstract: Purpose: Solid tumors harboring tumor mutational burden (TMB) ≥10 mutations per megabase (mut/Mb) received agnostic approval for pembrolizumab. This work aims to analyze the somatic mutational profile’s influence on the outcomes of patients with TMB-high tumors treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Methods: This post-hoc analysis evaluated clinical and molecular features of patients with solid tumors treated with ICIs that could be either monoclonal antibody directed against programmed cell death protein-1 or monoclonal antibody directed against programmed cell death ligand 1 (anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1), monoclonal antibody directed against cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen (anti-CTLA-4) or a combined treatment regimen including one anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 and one anti-CTLA-4 (ICIs combination). We performed OS analysis for TMB thresholds of ≥10, ≥20, and <10 mut/Mb. We assessed OS according to the mutational profile for a TMB ≥ 10 mut/Mb cutoff. For genes correlated with OS at the univariate assessment, we conducted a Cox multivariate analysis adjusted by median TMB, sex, age, microsatellite instability (MSI), and histology. Results: A total of 1661 patients were investigated; 488 with a TMB ≥10 mut/Mb (29.4%). The median OS was 42 months for TMB ≥10 or 20 mut/Mb, and 15 months for TMB <10 mut/Mb (p < 0.005). Among TMB ≥10 mut/Mb patients, mutations in E2F3 or STK11 correlated with worse OS, and mutations in NTRK3, PTPRD, RNF43, TENT5C, TET1, or ZFHX3 with better OS. These associations were confirmed with univariate and multivariate analyses (p < 0.05). Melanoma histology and TMB above the median endowed patients with better OS (p < 0.05), while MSI status, age, and gender did not have a statistically significant effect on OS. Conclusion: Combining TMB and mutation profiles in key cancer genes can better qualify patients for ICI treatment and predict their OS.

data.title: Impact of high tumor mutational burden in solid tumors and challenges for biomarker application.
data.abstract: Accurate identification of patients with solid tumors likely to respond to immunotherapy is crucial. Tumor mutational burden (TMB) measures the number of somatic mutations in a tumor and is an emerging prognostic and predictive biomarker for anti-programmed cell death (PD) 1/anti-PD-ligand 1 therapy and other immunotherapeutic agents. Tumor mutational burden is assessed optimally by whole exome sequencing, but next generation sequencing provides TMB estimates in a more timely and cost-effective manner. Blood-based measurement of TMB in plasma offers an alternative to the need for adequate tumor tissue for molecular testing, and has demonstrated the ability to identify patients who derive benefit from immunotherapy. Tumor mutational burden has diverse prognostic impact in different solid tumor types and also has a demonstrated role in predicting improved survival in patients receiving immunotherapy. There are challenges to TMB adoption into standard clinical practice, including variations in its definition, with the mutational number defining TMB-high appearing to vary across cancer types. The magnitude of TMB also varies across different tumor types, with the highest levels reported in melanoma and other skin cancers (where ultraviolet light is the dominant mutational process), followed by non-small cell lung cancer and other squamous carcinomas. Concerns regarding inter-laboratory and inter-platform variations in analysis methods have been raised, highlighting the need for standardization. Integration of other genomic or pathological biomarkers with TMB may increase its prognostic and predictive capabilities and validation of individual or combination models in prospective trials is warranted.

data.title: Predictive Impact of Tumor Mutational Burden on Real-World Outcomes of First-Line Immune Checkpoint Inhibition in Metastatic Melanoma.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
The choice of threshold and reliability of high tumor mutational burden (TMB) to predict outcomes and guide treatment choice for patients with metastatic melanoma receiving first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in the real world is not well known.
METHODS
Using a deidentified nationwide (US-based) melanoma clinicogenomic database, we identified a real-world cohort of patients with metastatic melanoma (N = 497) who received first-line monotherapy anti-PD-1 (n = 240) or dual anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4 ICI (n = 257) and had a tissue-based comprehensive genomic profiling test TMB score.
RESULTS
TMB-high (TMB-H; ≥10 mutations per megabase [muts/Mb], n = 352, 71%) was independently predictive of superior real-world progression-free survival and overall survival versus TMB-low (<10 mut/Mb, n = 145, 29%) in both mono ICI (hazard ratio [HR], 0.45 [95% CI, 0.32 to 0.63]; P < .001; HR, 0.61 [95% CI, 0.41 to 0.90]; P = .01, respectively) and dual ICI (HR, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.49 to 0.90]; P = .009; HR, 0.61 [95% CI, 0.42 to 0.88]; P = .007, respectively) patients. Dual ICI offered no significant advantage in BRAF wt patients and unexpectedly demonstrated greatest benefit in the TMB 10-19 mut/Mb group, identifying a TMB-very high (≥20 mut/Mb, n = 247, 50%) BRAF mut patient subgroup for whom mono ICI may be preferable.
CONCLUSION
TMB-H predicts superior outcomes on ICI while coassessment of BRAF status and TMB may inform first-line regimen choice.

data.title: Adjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy improves melanoma-specific survival in stage IIIC-IV melanoma patients with high tumor mutation burden and BRAF V600 mutation.
data.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) have significantly improved melanoma-specific survival (MSS), particularly in patients with tumors with a high tumor mutational burden (TMB) or BRAF mutation. In the adjuvant setting, ICIs significantly improve relapse-free survival (RFS), but data on MSS are still lacking. Tissue samples from 83 patients with stage IIIC/D/IV melanoma who started adjuvant ICI between March 2018 and September 2019 were examined using a 700 gene panel. TMB and BRAF V600E/K mutation status were analyzed to determine their potential influence on RFS and MSS. TMB levels ≥ 20 Var/Mb were classified as TMB high, corresponding to the top 20% TMB levels in the cohort. RFS and MSS were significantly improved in patients whose tumors had high TMB levels and BRAF V600E/K mutation (p<0.001 and p=0.002, respectively). Patients with BRAF -mutated tumors and high TMB seem to benefit particularly from adjuvant ICI.

data.title: Tumor mutation burden and circulating tumor DNA in combined CTLA-4 and PD-1 antibody therapy in metastatic melanoma - results of a prospective biomarker study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Metastasized or unresectable melanoma has been the first malignant tumor to be successfully treated with checkpoint inhibitors. Nevertheless, about 40-50% of the patients do not respond to these treatments and severe side effects are observed in up to 60%. Therefore, there is a high need to identify reliable biomarkers predicting response. Tumor Mutation Burden (TMB) is a debated predictor for response to checkpoint inhibitors and early measurement of ctDNA can help to detect treatment failure to immunotherapy in selected melanoma patients. However, it has not yet been clarified how TMB and ctDNA can be used to estimate response to combined CTLA-4 and PD-1 antibody therapy in metastatic melanoma.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
In this prospective biomarker study, we included 35 melanoma patients with ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) and nivolumab (anti-PD-1) therapy. In all patients, a tumor panel of 710 tumor-associated genes was applied (tumor vs. reference tissue comparison), followed by repetitive liquid biopsies. Cell-free DNA was extracted and at least one driver mutation was monitored. Treatment response was evaluated after about three months of therapy.
RESULTS
TMB was significantly higher in responders than in nonresponders and TMB > 23.1 Mut/Mb (TMB-high) was associated with a survival benefit compared to TMB ≤ 23.1 Mut/Mb (TMB-low or TMB-intermediate). Furthermore, a > 50% decrease of cell-free DNA concentration or undetectable circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), measured by tumor-specific variant copies/ml of plasma at first follow-up three weeks after treatment initiation were significantly associated with response to combined immunotherapy and improved overall survival, respectively. It is noticeable that no patient with TMB ≤ 23.1 Mut/Mb and detectable or increasing ctDNA at first follow-up responded to immunotherapy.
CONCLUSION
High TMB, > 50% decrease of cell-free DNA concentration, and undetectable ctDNA at first follow-up seem to be associated with response and overall survival under combined immunotherapy. The evaluation of ctDNA and cell-free DNA three weeks after treatment initiation may be suitable for early assessment of efficacy of immunotherapy.

data.title: ARID2 mutations may relay a distinct subset of cutaneous melanoma patients with different outcomes.
data.abstract: ARID genes encode subunits of SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes and are frequently mutated in human cancers. We investigated the correlation between ARID mutations, molecular features, and clinical outcomes in melanoma patients. Cutaneous melanoma samples (n = 1577) were analyzed by next-generation sequencing. Samples were stratified by pathogenic/likely pathogenic mutation in ARID genes (ARID1A/2/1B/5B). PD-L1 expression was assessed using IHC (SP142; positive (+): ≥ 1%). Tumor mutation burden (TMB)-high was defined as ≥ 10 mutations/Mb. Transcriptomic signatures predictive of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors-interferon gamma and T-cell inflamed score were calculated. Real-world overall survival (OS) information was obtained from insurance claims data, with Kaplan-Meier estimates calculated from time of tissue collection until last date of contact. Mann-Whitney U, Chi-square, and Fisher exact tests were applied where appropriate, with p values adjusted for multiple comparisons. ARID2 mutations were more prevalent in cutaneous melanoma compared to ARID1A (11.0%: n = 451 vs 2.8%: n = 113), with concurrent ARID1A/ARID2 mutation in 1.1% (n = 46) of samples. ARID mutations were associated with a high prevalence of RAS pathway mutations-NF1 (ARID1A, 52.6%; ARID2, 48.5%; ARID1A/2, 63.6%; and ARID-WT, 13.3%; p < 0.0001) and KRAS (ARID1A, 3.5%; ARID2, 3.1%; ARID1A/2, 6.5%; and ARID-WT, 1.0%; p = 0.018)), although BRAF mutations were less common in ARID-mutated cohorts (ARID1A, 31.9%; ARID2, 35.6%; ARID1A/2, 26.1%; and ARID-WT, 50.4%; p < 0.0001). TMB-high was more common in ARID-mutated samples (ARID1A, 80.9%; ARID2, 89.9%; ARID1A/2, 100%; and ARID-WT, 49.4%; p < 0.0001), while PD-L1 positivity was similar across subgroups (ARID1A, 43.8%; ARID2, 51.1%; ARID1A/2, 52.5%; and ARID-WT, 44.9%; p = 0.109). Patients with ARID1A mutations had a higher prevalence of dMMR/MSI-H compared to those with ARID-WT (2.7% vs 0.2%, p = 0.030). Median IFN-γ and T-cell signatures were higher in ARID2-mutated samples compared to ARID-WT (IFN-γ: - 0.15 vs - 0.21, p = 0.0066; T-cell: 23.5 vs - 18.5, p = 0.041). ARID2-mutated patients had improved survival compared to ARID-WT; (HR: 1.22 (95% CI 1.0-1.5), p = 0.022). No additional OS benefit was observed with anti-PD-1 therapy for ARID2 mutation compared to ARID-WT. Melanoma patients with ARID mutations exhibited higher prevalence of markers associated with ICI response, including TMB-H, and immune-related signatures. Our data also suggests improved survival outcome in patients with ARID2 mutations, irrespective of anti-PD1 therapy.

data.title: Clinical utility of tumor mutational burden in patients with non-small cell lung cancer treated with immunotherapy.
data.abstract: Anti-programmed death (ligand)-1 [anti-PD-(L)1] therapies such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab or atezolizumab have become standard of care for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients either in first line or beyond. PD-L1 expression level allows enriching the treated population with responders, but it is still not an optimal biomarker. Even in patients with PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) levels of ≥50% treated with first line pembrolizumab overall response rate (ORR) is only 44.8% and overall survival at one year is 70%. Moreover, in combination trials with chemotherapy and anti-PD-(L)1 therapy, a significant proportion of patients does not respond (ORR ranges from 45.3% to 64.0%), regardless of PD-L1 expression. Furthermore, PD-L1 expression level is not associated with improved benefit in patients treated with combinations of anti-PD-(L)1 and anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen (anti-CTLA4) therapy. One of the new promising biomarkers is tumor mutational burden (TMB). It has been discovered that especially tumor types with a known high mutation rate such as NSCLC and melanoma respond best to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). An explanation is that this high mutation rate makes it more likely that neoantigens arise that are targeted by activated immune cells, but it is not feasible to determine neoantigen load in daily practice. However, TMB of a certain tumor type is associated with neoantigen load and outcome on ICIs. In this comprehensive review, we discuss the TMB analysis methods, the rationale to use TMB as a predictive biomarker and the clinical utility of TMB in NSCLC patients treated with ICIs.

data.title: Biomarkers for Clinical Benefit of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Treatment-A Review From the Melanoma Perspective and Beyond.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) with anti-CTLA-4 and/or anti-PD-1 antibodies is standard treatment for metastatic melanoma. Anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) and anti-PD-L1 antibodies (atezolizumab, durvalumab, and avelumab) have been approved for treatment of several other advanced malignancies, including non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC); renal cell, and urothelial carcinoma; head and neck cancer; gastric, hepatocellular, and Merkel-cell carcinoma; and classical Hodgkin lymphoma. In some of these malignancies approval was based on the detection of biomarkers such as PD-L1 expression or high microsatellite instability.
METHODS
We review the current status of prognostic and predictive biomarkers used in ICI for melanoma and other malignancies. We include clinical, tissue, blood, and stool biomarkers, as well as imaging biomarkers.
RESULTS
Several biomarkers have been studied in ICI for metastatic melanoma. In clinical practice, pre-treatment tumor burden measured by means of imaging and serum lactate dehydrogenase level is already being used to estimate the likelihood of effective ICI treatment. In peripheral blood, the number of different immune cell types, such as lymphocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils, as well as different soluble factors, have been correlated with clinical outcome. For intra-tumoral biomarkers, expression of the PD-1 ligand PD-L1 has been found to be of some predictive value for anti-PD-1-directed therapy for NSCLC and melanoma. A high mutational load, particularly when accompanied by neoantigens, seems to facilitate immune response and correlates with patient survival for all entities treated by use of ICI. Tumor microenvironment also seems to be of major importance. Interestingly, even the gut microbiome has been found to correlate with response to ICI, most likely through immuno-stimulatory effects of distinct bacteria. New imaging biomarkers, e.g., for PET, and magnetic resonance imaging are also being investigated, and results suggest they will make early prediction of patient response possible.
CONCLUSION
Several promising results are available regarding possible biomarkers for response to ICI, which need to be validated in large clinical trials. A better understanding of how ICI works will enable the development of biomarkers that can predict the response of individual patients.

data.title: A PD-1/PD-L1 Proximity Assay as a Theranostic Marker for PD-1 Blockade in Patients with Metastatic Melanoma.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
Less than 50% of patients with melanoma respond to anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1), and this treatment can induce severe toxicity. Predictive markers are thus needed to improve the benefit/risk ratio of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). Baseline tumor parameters such as programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, CD8 + T-cell infiltration, mutational burden, and various transcriptomic signatures are associated with response to ICI, but their predictive values are not sufficient. Interaction between PD-1 and its main ligand, PD-L1, appears as a valuable target of anti-PD-1 therapy. Thus, instead of looking at PD-L1 expression only, we evaluated the predictive value of the proximity between PD-1 and its neighboring PD-L1 molecules in terms of response to anti-PD-1 therapy.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
PD-1/PD-L1 proximity was assessed by proximity ligation assay (PLA) on 137 samples from two cohorts (exploratory n = 66 and validation n = 71) of samples from patients with melanoma treated with anti-PD-1±anti-CTLA-4. Additional predictive biomarkers, such as PD-L1 expression (MELscore), CD8 + cells density, and NanoString RNA signature, were also evaluated.
RESULTS
A PD-1/PD-L1 PLA model was developed to predict tumor response in an exploratory cohort and further evaluated in an independent validation cohort. This score showed higher predictive ability (AUC = 0.85 and 0.79 in the two cohorts, respectively) for PD-1/PD-L1 PLA as compared with other parameters (AUC = 0.71-0.77). Progression-free and overall survival were significantly longer in patients with high PLA values ( P = 0.00019 and P < 0.0001, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS
The proximity between PD-1 and PD-L1, easily assessed by this PLA on one formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded section, appears as a new biomarker of anti-PD-1 efficacy.

trajectory.final_answer:
Summary

- Background: Tumor mutational burden (TMB) is an emerging biomarker that reflects the number of somatic mutations in a tumor and has been proposed to predict response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) across cancers, with melanoma historically having a high mutational load that may predispose to better immunogenicity and outcomes on immunotherapy. <cite id="32738738">Tumor mutational burden is an emerging prognostic and predictive biomarker for anti–PD-1/anti–PD-L1 therapy and other immunotherapeutic agents, with the highest TMB levels reported in melanoma and other skin cancers</cite>. <cite id="30002656">A high mutational load, particularly when accompanied by neoantigens, seems to facilitate immune response and correlates with patient survival in tumors treated with ICIs</cite>.

- Direct evidence in metastatic melanoma: In a large real-world cohort of 497 patients with metastatic melanoma treated with first-line anti–PD-1 alone or in combination with anti–CTLA-4, tissue TMB measured by comprehensive genomic profiling was independently associated with superior outcomes. Using a 10 mut/Mb cutoff to define TMB-high, TMB-high remained predictive of longer progression-free survival and overall survival in both monotherapy and combination ICI arms (PFS HR 0.45 and 0.67; OS HR 0.61 and 0.61, respectively), indicating that higher TMB is associated with benefit from ICIs in melanoma. <cite id="38848517">TMB-high (≥10 mut/Mb) was independently predictive of superior progression-free survival and overall survival versus TMB-low in both mono ICI and dual ICI patients</cite>.

- Additional supportive data: Prospective and adjuvant settings reinforce the link between high mutational burden and improved outcomes on immunotherapy, although thresholds and optimal integration with other biomarkers (e.g., BRAF status, MSI) remain under study. <cite id="31300034">In a prospective biomarker study of combined CTLA-4 and PD-1 therapy in melanoma, TMB>23.1 mut/Mb was associated with a survival benefit compared with TMB≤23.1 mut/Mb</cite>. <cite id="40874224">In adjuvant stage IIIC–IV melanoma, patients with BRAF V600E/K mutations and high TMB (≥20 mut/Mb) had significantly improved relapse-free and melanoma-specific survival on adjuvant ICI</cite>. <cite id="38848517">In metastatic melanoma, co-assessment of BRAF status and TMB may inform first-line regimen choice, with dual ICI offering no significant advantage in BRAF-wildtype patients and showing greatest benefit in the TMB 10–19 mut/Mb group, while TMB-very high (≥20 mut/Mb) BRAF-mutant patients may prefer monotherapy</cite>.

- Nuances and limitations: While TMB-high correlates with better outcomes on ICIs, TMB is heterogeneous across melanoma subsets, and predictive value varies with tumor context and therapy. <cite id="32738738">TMB’s predictive impact differs by cancer type, and practical challenges include inter-platform variability and the need for standardization and integration with other biomarkers</cite>. <cite id="38341515">Some high-TMB melanoma subsets (e.g., ARID2-mutant) may show improved survival independent of anti–PD-1 therapy, underscoring that TMB is part of a broader genomic and immune microenvironment context</cite>.

Answer to the question

- Does TMB predict an overall survival benefit from ICIs in metastatic melanoma? Based on real-world first-line melanoma data, higher TMB is independently associated with longer overall survival on immune checkpoint inhibitors, supporting TMB as a positive prognostic and potentially predictive marker of ICI benefit in metastatic melanoma. <cite id="38848517">TMB-high defined by ≥10 mut/Mb predicted superior overall survival in patients treated with anti–PD-1, both as monotherapy and in combination with anti–CTLA-4</cite>. <cite id="32738738">Mechanistically and clinically, melanoma’s high TMB aligns with improved outcomes on ICIs, consistent with the hypothesis that a higher mutational burden can enhance neoantigen presentation and immune recognition</cite>. <cite id="31300034">Prospective biomarker data in melanoma also associate higher TMB with survival benefit on combined CTLA-4/PD-1 therapy</cite>.

- Practical considerations and caveats: TMB thresholds and measurement platforms are not standardized across studies, and TMB should ideally be integrated with other biomarkers (e.g., BRAF, MSI) to guide therapy selection. <cite id="38848515">In metastatic melanoma, BRAF and TMB co-assessment may refine regimen choice, with dual ICI not showing a significant advantage in BRAF-wildtype patients and monotherapy potentially preferable in TMB-very-high BRAF-mutant tumors</cite>. <cite id="32738738">Broader adoption requires standardization and integration of TMB with other genomic and pathologic markers</cite>.

Bottom line

- Tumor mutational burden is associated with improved overall survival on immune checkpoint inhibitors in metastatic melanoma, particularly when TMB is high (e.g., ≥10 mut/Mb), and may help identify patients more likely to benefit from ICIs, though optimal thresholds, measurement standards, and integration with other biomarkers need further validation. <cite id="38848517">TMB-high predicts superior outcomes on ICI in metastatic melanoma</cite> <cite id="32738738">TMB-high melanomas tend to respond better to immunotherapy</cite> <cite id="31300034">High TMB correlates with survival benefit in combined ICI settings</cite>.
